Traverse about 250 yards across the northwest face on 3rd and 4th-class ledges to a 100 ft chimney just right of centre, then climb the route's eight technical pitches to where it joins Spontaneity Arete.
Finish on Spontaneity Arete's last one and a half scrambly ridge pitches, via the Goldie Crack, to the summit.
wa_fish_whistle: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles and turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road (FS Road 4065). Follow the gravel road about 2.3 miles to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, about 2,350 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Take Sunrise Mine Trail #707 across the South Fork Stillaguamish, up through Wirtz Basin and the loose, cairned couloir to Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft, then on to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan), the last water. Continue up the summit trail to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, leave it, and swing north across the slabs to the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, marked by two large cairns at about 5,700 ft with Copper Lake in view.

The heather ledges start on the 3rd-class slabs about 30 ft above the cairns. Follow the goat trail along them across the north face for roughly 800 ft to the notch where short 4th-class moves reach the original Ragged Edge start beside True Grit. The ledges are slick when wet and hold snow into midsummer.

Continue along the apron about 50 ft past the True Grit start to a large tree; the first pitch above it is a clean friction slab with five bolts in about 80 ft. Climb five pitches (5.10-), with cruxes on pitches 1, 3 and 5, to the top of the face.
The face tops out just below the summit; walk the last few feet to the top.
wa_flight_of_the_falcon: Walk the old roadbed past a flagged landslide crossing and the original road end to a wide, dry streambed of white boulders. Descend the bed about 200 ft, trend left into the alders to find the informal path, and follow it to the ford of Squire Creek, then on as the trail fades until the basin opens. Scramble the thin boulder-filled watercourse that comes down from the wall to the base beside Martha's Place, the huge overhung boulder.
wa_flycatcher_buttress: Hike up from the hairpin into the Spire Gully, following occasional cairns to the last large tree in the center of the gully, then traverse right across talus (snow early season) toward the gully that runs up to the notch between the two Early Winters Spires. Stay right of that dividing gully and scramble to the flat ledge at the start of the route.

Climb the ten pitches of the buttress (5.10b), taking the left of the two cracks on the pitch-6 crux and traversing left rather than going straight up off the pitch-8 belay; easy ground then leads to the summit plateau and the top.
wa_foggy_peak_scramble: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 30 miles past Verlot to Barlow Pass, where the pavement ends, and park at the trailhead at about 2,360 ft. The old Monte Cristo road beyond is gated to vehicles. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is available at the trailhead kiosk.
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges: From SR 20 at Marblemount, turn onto the Cascade River Road, which crosses the Skagit River and runs east, paved for about 10 miles and then rough gravel. Drive about 22 miles to a small pullout on the left beneath the northeast face of Johannesburg Mountain, at about 3,200 ft, with room for only a handful of cars. The road usually opens to its end by late June or early July. Overnight stays in the park require a backcountry permit.
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ridge: From SR 20 at Marblemount, turn onto the Cascade River Road, which crosses the Skagit River and runs east, paved for about 10 miles and then rough gravel. Drive about 22 miles to a small pullout on the left beneath the northeast face of Johannesburg Mountain, at about 3,200 ft, with room for only a handful of cars. The road usually opens to its end by late June or early July. Overnight stays in the park require a backcountry permit.

Follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about a mile and watch for the climbers' path leaving it. The path climbs steeply through forest with several creek crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft, then over talus and heather to the camps in Boston Basin.

From camp, do not head toward the south-face couloir; traverse east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies along the east side of the glacier below Forbidden. Expect hours of loose, choss-covered slabs, seepage and small stream crossings, usually finishing with a snow gully that wants crampons, then broken rock and snow up to the notch just above the high bivy, below the solitary gendarme.

From the notch, go left around the first gendarme and simul-climb easy blocks to the crest, then follow it west over the gendarmes rather than taking their bypasses. Rappel off the back of the last gendarme into a narrow notch, climb the 5.8 crux crack on the wall ahead, and continue on easier ground to the summit.
wa_forbidden_peak_north_ridge: From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into Boston Basin to the high camps near 6,400 ft.
wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face: From SR-20 in Marblemount, take the Cascade River Road (FS Road 15) east about 22 miles. Pavement ends near mile 10; the gravel beyond is potholed and gets narrow and steep near the end. The Boston Basin trailhead is a small pullout at about 3,200 ft, just before the Cascade Pass road-end lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and camping in Boston Basin requires a park backcountry permit.

From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into Boston Basin to the high camps near 6,400 ft.
wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face: From SR-20 in Marblemount, take the Cascade River Road (FS Road 15) east about 22 miles. Pavement ends near mile 10; the gravel beyond is potholed and gets narrow and steep near the end. The Boston Basin trailhead is a small pullout at about 3,200 ft, just before the Cascade Pass road-end lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and camping in Boston Basin requires a park backcountry permit.

From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into Boston Basin to the high camps near 6,400 ft.
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge: From SR-20 in Marblemount, take the Cascade River Road (FS Road 15) east about 22 miles. Pavement ends near mile 10; the gravel beyond is potholed and gets narrow and steep near the end. The Boston Basin trailhead is a small pullout at about 3,200 ft, just before the Cascade Pass road-end lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park, and camping in Boston Basin requires a park backcountry permit.

From the pullout, follow the old Diamond Mine roadbed about a mile, then take the unsigned climbers' path that leaves it and climbs steeply through forest, crossing four streams, to treeline near 5,300 ft. Continue up heather and boulder slopes into the Boston Basin cirque to the camps.

Make an ascending traverse up and east across talus and the glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face, roping up if it is snow-covered or crevassed; when it is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often faster. Climb the obvious 500 ft snow couloir on the left edge of the south face, steepening to 40-50 degrees past a moat near the top, to the notch on the crest. Late season, use the loose Cat Scratch gullies just left of it.

From the notch, climb steep blocks onto the crest and follow it to climber's right over the air step and a series of gendarmes and knife edges, about six pitches of low fifth class. Take the crux tower two-thirds of the way up on its left side, continue along the narrowing crest to a false summit, downclimb about 10 ft of exposed rock, and make easy moves to the true summit.
wa_free_mojo: The Blue Lake trailhead is on the south side of SR-20 near milepost 162, about a mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail to the clearing on the northwest side of the spires, then take the climbers' path up talus into the basin below the west face. Free Mojo starts on a plain crack about 40 ft down and right of the big chockstone-filled chimney between the two formations, and six pitches lead to the summit.
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles to Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road), turn east and drive about 6.4 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead parking lot at about 2,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.

Gain the Kennedy Glacier, a crumbling mess of moraine and big boulders at its toe, and climb it roped to the 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite Ridge begins. Follow the crest over pumice and 45-50 degree snow to the Rabbit Ears, pass through their notch and downclimb about 150 ft of class 3, then climb one to two pitches of alpine ice to the crater rim. Cross the crater and climb its far wall to the summit.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles to Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road), turn east and drive about 6.4 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead parking lot at the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles to Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road), turn east and drive about 6.4 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead parking lot at about 2,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.

Follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter at about 5.5 miles, then climb a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail in meadows at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8.5 miles from the car.

Turn north on the PCT over Red Pass and follow it down the upper White Chuck valley 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction, to a forest camp near 4,100 ft by Sitkum Creek. Take the unsigned climbers' path straight up the ridge south of the creek to Boulder Basin, then head southeast up snowfields onto the Sitkum Glacier, climb it to the 9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, and follow the pumice ridge to the summit.
wa_goat_mountain_east_peak: From the Glacier Public Service Center, drive SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) east 12.5 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32). Follow it 2.3 miles to the Goat Mountain Trailhead at about 2,470 ft, with parking on both sides of the road. A Northwest Forest Pass or other valid recreation pass is required.
wa_golden_horn_north_face: Drive SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass and park at the Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of the highway, at about 4,860 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park. The highway over the pass closes in winter.

Follow the PCT north about 5 miles to Cutthroat Pass and 2.4 miles more to Granite Pass, then about 2.2 miles on to a small, easily missed spur that climbs about 500 ft in half a mile to Snowy Lakes at about 6,700 ft. From the lakes travel northwest into Golden Horn's basin to reach the north face, and climb the face to the summit.
wa_golden_horn_southwest_route: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Rainy Pass near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount, and park at the Rainy Pass North trailhead for the Pacific Crest Trail at about 4,880 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail over Cutthroat Pass and past Granite Pass, then along the cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. About a mile before Methow Pass, take the spur that switchbacks up to Lower and then Upper Snowy Lake. From the lakes, scramble loose class 2-3 scree and talus on the southwest flank to the summit ridge, then make the short, exposed move across the gap onto the summit block.
wa_goode_mountain_megalodon_ridge: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Bridge Creek Trailhead near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, and park in the paved lot on the north side of the highway at about 4,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and an NPS backcountry permit is needed for overnight camping.

Cross the highway on the connector and hike the PCT south 9-10 miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail junction, then up the brushy North Fork trail. Leave it for a steep bushwhack through slide alder and timber to the toe of the clean arete running northeast off the main ridge, with no glacier crossing. Climb the ridge over the 8,200 ft tower and the Southeast Peak to Black Tooth Notch, then easier pitches to the summit.
wa_goode_mountain_northeast_face: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Bridge Creek Trailhead near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass, and park in the lot at about 4,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and an NPS backcountry permit is needed for overnight camping.

Cross the highway on the connector and hike the PCT south about 9.6 miles along Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail junction, then turn up the North Fork trail. Ford the North Fork and bushwhack up to a camp near the Goode Glacier moraine at about 6,700 ft. From camp, rope up and cross the Goode Glacier to the base of the face, and climb it to the summit.
wa_goode_mountain_southwest_couloir: Cross SR-20 on the connector trail and hike the Pacific Crest Trail south along Bridge Creek, losing elevation steadily through forest for about 9.5 miles to the North Fork Camp junction. Turn off the PCT here onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail.
Head upstream on the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail to the Grizzly Creek crossing, usually an easy log but a high, hard-to-find ford in early season.

Continue up the North Fork trail as it grows brushier, then leave the tread and ford the North Fork, easiest a short way upstream near a cairn. Follow an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder tunnels, then climb heather and scree to the lateral moraine above the Goode Glacier.
Leave camp across the moraine and onto the glacier remnant toward the couloir. Route-finding is tricky and late-season snow bridges can be rotten, so rope up.

Scramble talus and loose scree to the rotten ridge below the couloir and the narrow cairned ledge that leads into it. Climb the couloir on the solid dark rock of the black stairs along its left side, class 3-4 with a short low fifth-class step low down, to Black Tooth Notch, gained by an exposed class 4 traverse with a fixed sling at the crux step.
From the notch, traverse across the upper Northeast Face and climb the exposed class 4-5 summit block to the true top.
wa_gothic_peak_standard: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east past the Verlot Public Service Center and continue 19.3 miles beyond it to Barlow Pass, where the pavement ends, and park at the Barlow Pass Trailhead at about 2,360 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park.

Walk past the gate and follow the closed Monte Cristo road about a mile, then fork right into the forest onto the Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail #724. Ford Weden Creek, climb the steep root-and-rock switchbacks out of the timber into Gothic Basin, then continue up slabs and talus to the saddle above Foggy Lake and drop down to the lake.

From the lake's outlet, follow the cairned climber's path up Gothic's southeast ridge, staying in the scree climber's right of the crest, past a small tarn at the foot of a snowfield and up broken rock to the base of the summit block. Cut left onto a narrow downsloping ledge and switchback back right to the block for the final short class 3 scramble; exposed class 4 rock further left is off route.
wa_gunrunner: From Darrington, drive north on SR 530 about 8 miles to the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26) and follow it east about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead at about 1,440 ft, just past the Downey Creek bridge. Park on the south side of the road; the trail starts on the north side. A Northwest Forest Pass or the $5 day fee is required to park.

Hike the Downey Creek Trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing and follow the climbers' path up Bachelor Creek to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge. Rope up for the Dome Glacier to the Dome-Chickamin col, then cross the Chickamin Glacier beneath the Gunsight peaks to the north end of the ridge. Climb the crest over the Northeast and North peaks to Gunsight Notch, then a dihedral on the east side of the crest to Middle Peak.
wa_gunsight_peak_standard: From Darrington, drive SR-530 north about 8 miles and turn east onto the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26). Follow it about 20 miles to the Downey Creek bridge; the trail starts just past the bridge on the north side, with parking on the south side at about 1,450 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee and a free self-issue wilderness permit are required. Washouts have closed this road short of the trailhead for long periods, so check its status first.
wa_hadley_peak_cougar_divide: From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 7.5 miles to the Wells Creek / Nooksack Falls junction near milepost 41 and turn right onto gravel FS Road 33. Stay on the main road roughly 12 miles to its end at an unsigned parking area in an old clearcut at about 4,900 ft. The last miles are rocky and cross-ditched, so high clearance helps, and the road is gated seasonally from November into early July. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Follow Cougar Divide Trail #601 south along the divide, through meadow and forest with some up and down, about 2.7 miles to the trail's high point near 5,900 ft where the tread ends. Continue cross-country up about 1,000 ft to the crest of Chowder Ridge, then follow the climbers' path along the ridge, sidehilling on steep, loose ground, to the base of Hadley's summit block. A short, loose hard Class 3 scramble reaches the tiny summit.
wa_hadley_peak_skyline_divide: From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 1 mile past the Glacier Public Service Center, turn right onto Glacier Creek Road (FS Road 39), then immediately left onto Deadhorse Road (FS Road 37). Follow FS 37 about 13 miles to the trailhead lot at its end. FS 37 has been closed by a flood washout near milepost 3 since 2021, so check its status before planning to drive to the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Climb Skyline Divide Trail #678 through old-growth switchbacks to meadows on the ridge crest at about 2 miles, then follow the crest south to the trail's high point near 6,500 ft at about 4.5 miles; note it, since it is where you rejoin the trail on the way back. Continue cross-country along the open crest, roughly 3 miles, onto Chowder Ridge and along it to the base of Hadley's summit block, then make the short, loose hard Class 3 scramble to the summit.
wa_half_moon_southwest_slopes: Climb the loose talus and scree gully that angles back east to the deep notch just north of Half Moon, keeping the party close together to limit rockfall. From the notch, climb the North Ridge, about seven pitches on or just west of the crest, belaying at the obvious ledges, to an easy scramble to the summit.
wa_himmelhorn_southeast_route: From the Himmel-Otto col, follow a ledge onto the north face and continue up the northwest side, mostly scrambling with short steeper steps of Class 4 to low fifth class, to the 7,880 ft summit.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_north_peak_north_ro: From Trans-Canada Highway 1 just west of Hope, B.C., take Exit 168 to Flood Hope Road and turn onto the Silver Skagit Road, following it about 36 miles (58 km) south to its end at the border and the Hozomeen ranger station and campground at the head of Ross Lake. The border gate there has been closed to vehicles and walkers; confirm it is open before planning on this drive.

From the ranger station follow the short Trail of the Obelisk loop, leave it heading east, cross Howlett Creek and climb cross-country up the forested west flank to a heathery knoll near 5,900 ft on the north ridge. Follow the ridge south over several bumps, drop about 250 ft into the north cirque, climb its snowfields and loose ramps to the northeast ridge ledges near 7,600 ft, and make the exposed Class 4 moves to the summit.
wa_hozomeen_mountain_southeast_face: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking at about milepost 134. There is no public road to the Hozomeen end of the lake from the south; walk down from here to Ross Lake Resort for its water taxi.

Take the water taxi about 24 miles north to Hozomeen at the head of the lake, then follow the Hozomeen Lake Trail and leave it near the lake's outlet at about 2,400 ft. Cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east through devil's club and deadfall, up a chockstone-choked gully near 5,000 ft and red scree past a slab wall to the saddle camp near 6,800 ft, then slabs and gullies to the southeast face and the summit.
wa_icy_peak_southwest_route: Follow the Hannegan Pass Trail (#674) about 3.5 miles up the Ruth Creek valley through forest and avalanche meadows to the signed spur for Hannegan Camp. Fill water here; there is no reliable running water beyond it.
Continue up the trail about half a mile of switchbacks to the broad meadow of Hannegan Pass.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the dusty gully toward Ruth Mountain, then along the heather ridge skirting a minor peak, to where it drops onto the lowest snow finger of the Ruth Glacier.
Rope up and climb the moderate slopes of the Ruth Glacier to Ruth Mountain's summit plateau. Crevasses open on the upper glacier in late season.
Descend Ruth's south side toward the Ruth-Icy saddle on the cairned heather slopes and game trail to climber's left, avoiding the steep, loose gully that is the natural fall line.
From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to the edge of the Icy Glacier and rope up again.

Climb the glacier's northwest slope gradually southeast with the rock ridge on your left and the crevasses on your right to about 6,500 ft, then step through the notch west of the Northwest Spire. About 500 ft of Class 2-3 talus and snow lead to a light-colored 100-ft Class 4 gully and the northwest summit; the higher southeast tower takes more Class 3-4 scrambling.
wa_indian_head_peak_southwest_slopes: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles to Forest Road 49 (Sloan Creek Road). Turn east and drive about 6.5 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead parking at the road's end. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park.
wa_indian_mountain_baker_scramble: From Glacier, drive SR 542, the Mt. Baker Highway, about 13 miles east and turn left onto FS Road 32 just before the bridge over the Nooksack River. At 1.3 miles keep left on Ruth Creek Road and continue about 5.4 miles to the road end at Hannegan Campground. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park.
wa_inspiration_traverse: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto the Cascade River Road and drive about 20 miles east, paved for the first 10 then rough gravel, to the Eldorado parking area on the right near milepost 20. The climbers' trail leaves the road a short walk west of the lot. A free backcountry permit from the park is required for any overnight stay.
wa_jack_mountain_nohokomeen_headwall: Cross the Ruby Creek bridge below the lot and follow the flat East Bank Trail about 8 miles north along Ross Lake to May Creek Camp. Leave the trail there and climb the steep timber between the creeks, threading the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft on boot and game trails; snow usually begins near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and about 3 miles of this reaches a flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the glacier.

Climb the glacier roped, around the crevassed and icefall sections low down, to the head of the gentle bowl directly below the summit. Cross the bergschrund, climb the headwall on sustained snow that steepens to as much as 60 degrees near the top, then exit onto the narrow corniced summit ridge and traverse it to the true summit, keeping well back from the cornice.
wa_jack_mountain_north_ridge: Drive SR 20 east from Newhalem to the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138, at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops from the lot to the bridge over Ruby Creek.

Follow the East Bank Trail north along Ross Lake to May Creek Camp, then climb steep forest on game trails through the rock bands to the ridge crest near 5,000 ft. Pass under the Nohokomeen Glacier's toe to camp on slabs on its left side, climb the glacier's centre right of the large rock to about 8,000 ft, squeeze through the keyhole onto the knife-edge crest, traverse snow south below the summit tower, and finish up the East Ridge.
wa_jack_mountain_northeast_glacier: Drive SR 20 east from Newhalem to the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138, at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops from the lot to the bridge over Ruby Creek.
wa_jack_mountain_southeast_ridge_direct: Drive SR 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, about 33 miles east of Marblemount, at about 1,900 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, and a free self-issued permit is required to enter the Pasayten Wilderness.

Cross Canyon Creek, judging the crossing first, and climb Trail #738's switchbacks about 3.7 miles to the Crater Lake junction, carrying water. Leave the trail between 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the 7,200 ft saddle on Crater Mountain, descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, and cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes to camp. From camp climb to the level step on the southeast ridge at 7,000 to 7,200 ft and stay on the crest to the summit.
wa_jack_mountain_southwest_ridge: Follow the East Bank Trail about 2.4 miles to a junction where several ways meet and take the rightmost branch, the old unmaintained Little Jack trail; if you are still on level ground along the lake well past the junction, you took the wrong branch. It climbs steadily, about 4,800 ft, to the open, meadowy top of Little Jack at 6,745 ft, about 6 miles from the car. Carry water from low down.

Follow the crest northeast from Little Jack to the notch and stay on the ridge rising ahead. Climb Class 2-3 ground, make a short Class 4 downclimb past a subpeak, then continue on Class 3 crest over a cairned false summit to the high point at the southwest corner of the Nohokomeen Glacier. Finish east-northeast along the shattered ridge on the glacier's rim to the summit.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_cj_couloir: Walk back down the road from the trailhead, anywhere from a quarter mile to just under a mile, then drop down a dirt and brush embankment into the valley and cross the Cascade River, often still snow-covered in spring. Cross the terminal moraine and a snowfield to the continuous snow apron at the foot of the couloir, about twenty minutes from the road.

Climb about 3,000 ft of snow up the couloir, moving early and never stopping in the choke, where a bulge of water ice may need a belay or can sometimes be passed on a narrower line to the right. Above the choke go up and left, then straight up the final couloir to the Cascade-Johannesburg col; a cornice there has been passed against the rock of Cascade Peak on the left.

From the col climb the steep east side on heather, talus and broken rock bands, mostly Class 3-4, past rock horns to a red dike, then up a steep gray gully of about 500 ft to the false summit. Drop about 30 ft and traverse loose south-side ledges roughly 75 ft below the crest, in and out of ribs and gullies, to a deep slot-gully that gives a final Class 3-4 pitch to the true summit.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_rib_1: From SR-20 at Marblemount, keep straight where the highway turns left and you are on Cascade River Road. Follow it about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead lot, around 3,600 ft; the upper road is gravel. No parking pass is needed for day use, but a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is required to camp on the route.

From the lot, drop to and cross the Cascade River, cross the terminal moraine, and downclimb into the avalanche moat to gain the rock before the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir narrows. Climb the Northeast Rib through brush, heather and about 700 ft of good 5.6 rock to the bivy ledge near 7,100 ft, then the snow arete and headwall above, and scramble Class 3 along the summit ridge to the top.
wa_katsuk_peak_gully: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur signed for Easy Pass, ending at a lot for about 10 cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required (self-issue at the kiosk). The highway closes in winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it opens for the season.
wa_kimtah_peak_scramble: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur signed for Easy Pass, ending at a lot for about 10 cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required (self-issue at the kiosk). The highway closes in winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it opens for the season.
Climb the gully on solid class 3 granite, often holding snow or meltwater, to the ridge crest, then cross the scree saddle and scramble class 3 rock along the crest to the true (east) summit.
wa_klawatti_peak_southeast_face: Find the current log crossing of the Cascade River (it shifts from year to year, so scout up- and downstream if it is gone), then follow the unmaintained climbers' path as it switchbacks steeply through timber and brush for about 1,500 ft to the start of the cairned talus field, with cliffs on the left.

Cross the boulders staying climber's right, since cairn lines trending left lead into cliffier ground. Follow the climbers' trail up a rib to a basin at 5,500-5,800 ft, drop slightly into the Roush Creek drainage for the last reliable running water, then climb again to the camps at 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier.
Rope up at camp and climb the snowfields above onto the Eldorado Glacier, keeping just west (left) of the rocky ridge above the basin.
Climb the crevassed Eldorado Glacier north to the broad Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap and the high camp near the base of Eldorado's east ridge.

Clear the bergschrund on a short class 4 to low-fifth rock step, or a snow bridge if one holds, then climb several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow to the top of the face. From there the elongated summit crest is an easy scramble; its true high point is hard to pick out.
wa_klawatti_peak_sw_buttress: Cross the Cascade River near the trailhead on whatever log or ford is in that year, then climb the steep, unmaintained climbers' path through old growth to the boulder field and on into the Eldorado Creek and Roush Creek basin. Rope up there and climb the Eldorado Glacier to camp on the ice cap near the base of Eldorado's east ridge.

Roped, traverse the Inspiration Glacier north-northeast past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col, the saddle between the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on the peak's south side. The ice cap is flat and featureless and whiteouts are common, so carry a bearing or track.

The buttress stands minutes above the col camp. Cross the moat onto the rock, climb one to three short low-fifth pitches of loose rock up the buttress, then scramble along the elongated southwest crest to the summit, where the high point is not obvious.
wa_koala_krack: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the large turnout at the hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass, at about 5,100 ft, the same pullout used for the Hairpin and Kangaroo Ridge climbs. The highway closes in winter, so it is reachable only once it opens for the season.

Walk south across the boulder field and follow the faint, intermittently cairned climbers' path through forest and talus to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour. From the pass, traverse the on-and-off trail to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger and climb it toward the notch, finish one of the face routes, then take Koala Krack, the wide left-trending crack on the summit block, to the top.
wa_kololo_peaks_standard: From the four-way stop in Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles and turn left onto FS Road 49, the North Fork Sauk Road. Follow it about 6.4 miles to the large trailhead lot near the road end at about 2,050 ft, where North Fork Sauk Trail #649 begins. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is filled out at the kiosk.
wa_labor_pains: Drive SR 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park. The highway over the pass closes in winter.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail and take the climbers' path into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group. Continue past South Early Winters Spire to the west side of the two Early Winters Spires and the base of the big chasm between them, where the Chockstone Route starts.
wa_le_conte_mountain_northern_aspect: Hike the Cascade Pass Trail about 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft of gain up long switchbacks to the pass.

From the pass, leave the trail and head south up Mixup Arm on the climbers' path, then traverse to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. Climb its moderate snow slopes to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft. Expect glacier travel.

Descend to Kool-Aid Lake, pass the Red Ledge, cross the Middle Cascade Glacier to the Spider-Formidable col and drop to camp at the Yang Yang Lakes. From camp, climb the ridge south by the secret stair to the outcrop below the north face, bypass Peak 7004 on its east slope, then take a loose gully and short snow near 7,200 ft to the east notch and an exposed ledge traverse to the summit.
wa_lexington_tower_east_face: From Washington Pass on SR 20, drive about 1.2 miles east and downhill to the hairpin turn. Park at the small dirt pullout beside a roadside pond on the south side of the highway. The highway over the pass closes in winter.

Take the climbers' path from just west of the east-side guardrail, steeply through forest onto a scree and boulder slope below the east face, 30 to 45 minutes. Gain the treed ledge at the base by a roped 5.8 pitch or a flanking gully, climb the ten-pitch East Face (5.9+), and finish with the exposed catwalk traverse to the notch below the true summit.
wa_liberty_and_injustice_for_all: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Washington Pass and continue east down from the pass to the big hairpin turn below Liberty Bell's East Face, at about 5,200 ft; coming from Winthrop it is the hairpin just before the final climb to the pass. Park on the shoulder at the curve, then walk back up the road toward the pass to a small pond on the south side, where the climbers' path starts at its east end. SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.
wa_liberty_bell_beckey_route: Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow just past a stream crossing, the last reliable water, and turn left onto the climbers' path. It climbs steeply through granite slabs, talus and heather into the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch; where the path forks a couple hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch up loose scree to the notch at about 7,300 ft. The gully often holds snow into late June.

From the notch, climb the Beckey Route up Liberty Bell's southwest side: a chimney to a ledge with a tree anchor, then the crux chimney past big chockstones, 4th-class ground to a short finger-crack traverse around a roof protected by a fixed pin, and a dihedral back right onto the summit shoulder. A slabby 10-ft 5.6 move and easy scrambling finish on the summit.
wa_liberty_bell_girl_next_door: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 31 miles; the Blue Lake Trailhead is on the left a little under a mile past the Washington Pass Overlook (from the west, about 42 miles from Newhalem, on the right before the overlook). The lot is small and fills early on summer weekends; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required, and SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow just past a small stream crossing and turn left onto the climbers' path up slabs, talus and meadow into the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. A couple hundred feet below the notch, walk partway up the side gully on climber's left with a large cave and step right onto a treed ledge to start. Climb the three pitches to the top of the arete and follow the Beckey Route finish to the summit.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Washington Pass and continue east down from the pass to the big hairpin turn below Liberty Bell's East Face, at about 5,200 ft; coming from Winthrop it is the hairpin just before the final climb to the pass. Park on the north shoulder at the curve, then walk back up the road toward the pass to a small pond on the south side, where the climbers' path starts at its east end. SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.
wa_liberty_bell_overexposure: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 31 miles; the Blue Lake Trailhead is on the left a little under a mile past the Washington Pass Overlook (from the west, about 42 miles from Newhalem, on the right before the overlook). A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required, there is a privy at the lot, and SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.
wa_liberty_bell_serpentine_crack: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 31 miles; the Blue Lake Trailhead is on the left a little under a mile past the Washington Pass Overlook (from the west, about 42 miles from Newhalem, on the right before the overlook). A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required, there is a privy at the lot, and SR-20 is closed over the pass in winter.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow just past a small stream crossing and turn left onto the climbers' path up slabs and talus into the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch; where the gully forks, stay left and cache packs. Scramble 4th-class ledges to a slung small pine above slabs at the base of the crack, climb the four pitches, then simul-climb the exposed arete to the summit.
wa_liberty_bell_sidewinder: Drive SR-20 to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the cairned climbers' trail junction, then take the climbers' path up talus and slabs into the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, breaking left at the fork to the shelf and ramp below the cave at the base of the southwest corner. Climb the crack pitches and finish on 4th-class scrambling to the summit.
wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line: From the east end of the pond, follow the cairned climbers' path as it climbs steeply through forest to the talus and snow below the East Face. The start is right of Liberty Crack and is best picked out from the talus by tracing the line down from features higher on the wall; climb the lower pitches to the sustained corner and thin-crack pitches.
Above the crux corners, continue up the crack pitches to M&M Ledge, then easier corners and ledges on the upper apron, and finish with easy scrambling to the true summit.
wa_liberty_crack_free: Drive SR-20 to the large hairpin turn just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve. Walk back up the road toward the pass to the small pond on the south side of the highway, where the climbers' path starts.
wa_liberty_traverse: Drive SR-20 to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' junction just past a small stream, marked by a large cairn, then climb the path up slabs, talus and heather into the gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Keep climber's left low in the gully, cross right higher up, and take the left fork a couple of hundred feet below the notch to the Beckey Route start; four short pitches lead to the summit.
wa_lincoln_peak_north_ridge: From Glacier on the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542), drive about 1 mile east and turn right onto Glacier Creek Road (FS Road 39). Follow it about 8 miles to the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead parking on the left side of the road. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.
wa_little_mac_spire_southwest_route: From SR-20 at Newhalem, turn north onto the gravel road across the highway from the Newhalem Campground and follow signs toward the Goodell Creek group camp; park at the small turnout at the trailhead just before the camp.

Follow the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' trail north along the old, overgrown logging road bed paralleling Goodell Creek. The walking is forested and comparatively gentle to the creek crossings.
Continue along the old road bed to its end, where a large cairn and stone arrow mark a hard right turn uphill onto the Terror Basin climbers' path.

Turn right and climb the path, which goes brutally steeply more or less straight up the timbered ridge nose between Terror and Crescent Creeks, through brush and a class 3 root-pull cliff band, to the rocky streambed where the last dependable water runs.
Pick up the faint tread just upstream and make a rising traverse, over moderate snow into midsummer, to the 6,200 ft gap on the east rim of Terror Basin.
Drop down the scree or snow on the far side of the notch to the flat gravel benches of camp at about 5,800 ft.
wa_little_sister_north_face: From SR 9 north of Sedro-Woolley, turn right onto Mosquito Lake Road just after crossing the South Fork Nooksack and drive about 9 miles. Just past the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, turn right onto FR 38 and drive about 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking across the road. The road is gated at Wallace Creek, 1.3 miles short, from Dec 1 to Jun 15. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required.

Cross the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack on a log (most parties use one about a quarter mile downstream of the marked ford) and follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 about 1.5 miles to the blue-diamond Green Creek climbers' path. Follow it up the brushy Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress near 3,800 ft, over scree and slabs onto the Green Creek Glacier, and up the glacier to where it ends against the north face.
wa_little_sister_south_couloir: From SR 9 north of Sedro-Woolley, turn right onto Mosquito Lake Road just after crossing the South Fork Nooksack and drive about 9 miles. Just past the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, turn right onto FR 38 and drive about 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking across the road. The road is gated at Wallace Creek, 1.3 miles short, from Dec 1 to Jun 15. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required.

Cross the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack on whatever log is in place, follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 about 1.5 miles and take the blue-diamond Green Creek climbers' path up the valley, past the buttress near 3,800 ft and onto the Green Creek Glacier. Climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, then traverse onto the south side and climb the snow and rock gully to the top.
wa_little_sister_west_face: From SR 9 north of Sedro-Woolley, turn right onto Mosquito Lake Road just after crossing the South Fork Nooksack and drive about 9 miles. Just past the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, turn right onto FR 38 and drive about 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking across the road. The road is gated at Wallace Creek, 1.3 miles short, from Dec 1 to Jun 15. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required.
wa_lizard_mountain_south_route: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto the Cascade River Road and follow it about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (about 3,600 ft); the upper road is narrow gravel. No parking pass is needed, but camping inside North Cascades National Park on the way to White Rock Lakes requires a park backcountry permit.
wa_luna_glacier: From SR 20 at Marblemount, drive east about 28 miles, past Newhalem and Diablo Lake, to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking near milepost 134.

Drop 0.8 mile to the service road, cross Ross Dam and follow the trail about 6 miles north along Ross Lake to Big Beaver Creek (or take the water taxi to Big Beaver landing), then the Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp. Go cross-country into Luna Cirque, climb the hanging glacier directly south of Phantom to where it narrows, turn north over a rock step to the top snowfield, and follow slabs to the ridge and the summit block.
wa_magic_mountain_north_face: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto the Cascade River Road and follow it about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (about 3,600 ft); the upper road is narrow gravel.
From the road-end parking, the maintained trail switchbacks up through forest and then traverses meadow and talus for about 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass.

Cross the pass and descend east about half a mile to Pelton Basin. Climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier, rope up and follow it southwest to the Magic-Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. Bear back west across the head of the glacier to the north face, climb about 600 ft of steep Class 4 rock to the notch just northwest of the summit, and scramble to the top.
wa_magic_mountain_northeast_couloir: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up its long series of switchbacks through forest and then open meadow slopes for 3.7 miles to the broad saddle of Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft.

Cross the pass and descend east about half a mile to Pelton Basin. Climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier, rope up, and follow the glacier southwest to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. The northeast couloir rises directly above the col; climb it on snow, about 40-45 degrees low and 45-50 near the top, to the summit.
wa_magic_mountain_northwest_ridge: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up its long series of switchbacks for 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft.

Take the Ptarmigan Traverse climbers' path south across Mixup Peak's flanks to the Cache Glacier, climb it to Cache Col near 6,900 ft and descend about 600 ft toward Kool-Aid Lake. Walk the easy southwest slopes to the base of the ridge, climb steep broken rock and an easy chimney to the notch just northwest of the summit, then traverse and climb the short northwest face to the top.
wa_magic_mountain_southwest_cirque: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River and follow the Cascade River Road 23.1 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead, near 3,600 ft. The road is paved for the first third, then gravel with narrow, steep sections near the top, and usually opens all the way to the trailhead only around the end of June. An overnight stay in the park requires a backcountry permit.
Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up its long series of switchbacks for 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft.

Take the Ptarmigan Traverse climbers' path south across Mixup Peak's flanks to the Cache Glacier, climb it to Cache Col near 6,900 ft and descend about 600 ft toward Kool-Aid Lake, then trend into the cirque southwest of the summit rather than continuing to the Magic–Hurry-up col. Climb one of the heathery gullies at the north or northeast head of the cirque to the summit ridge and scramble the crest to the top.
wa_magic_mountain_west_ridge: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River and follow the Cascade River Road 23.1 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead, near 3,600 ft. The road is paved for the first third, then gravel with narrow, steep sections near the top, and usually opens all the way to the trailhead only around the end of June. An overnight stay in the park requires a backcountry permit.
Follow the Cascade Pass Trail up its long series of switchbacks for 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft.

Take the Ptarmigan Traverse climbers' path across Mixup Peak's flanks, climb the Cache Glacier to Cache Col near 6,900 ft and descend toward the Kool-Aid Lake basin. Easy west-southwest slopes lead to the pocket glacier under the west face; cross the bergschrund, climb shelves, the 5.6 open book and the slab's left side, then an easy chimney to the crest between the false and main summits, and scramble to the top.
wa_marvin_s_ear: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles (17.1 miles past the Verlot Public Service Center) and turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road, FS Road 4065. Follow this rough gravel road about 2.2 miles to the trailhead at its end, near 2,350 ft; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
wa_mcgregor_mountain_scramble: There is no road to this trailhead from outside: reach Stehekin at the head of Lake Chelan by the Lady of the Lake ferry, floatplane or trail, then ride the valley shuttle, bike or walk 11 miles up the Stehekin Valley Road from Stehekin Landing to High Bridge, around 1,600 ft. Arrange any overnight backcountry permit before you travel, since there is no permit office in Stehekin.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_southwest_ridge: Drive SR-20 to Newhalem and turn off at the Goodell Creek Campground just west of town, around milepost 119, to the Upper Goodell Group Campground trailhead at about 600 ft. The unsigned climbers' path starts behind a large boulder near the campground. Overnight stays require a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Follow the old Goodell Creek roadbed about 4 miles to the cairned turnoff, climb roughly 4,000 ft to heather benches and go north to the 6,200 ft notch, then descend its loose north side, staying skier's right, to Terror Basin camp. Traverse benches and slabs to the glacial lake outlet, climb onto the Terror Glacier and continue to its east end, where the southwest ridge rises about six pitches to the summit.
wa_mcmillan_spire_west_west_ridge: From camp, make a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, to the outlet of the glacial lake, then climb the slabs above it onto the Terror Glacier remnant. The crossing is short and low-angle, but it can show bare ice by late summer.
wa_mojo_rising: Drive SR-20 to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway about a mile west of Washington Pass, between mileposts 161 and 162, roughly 42 miles east of Newhalem. The paved lot requires a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee. The highway is closed in winter.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1 to 1.25 miles to the clearing on its northwest side, then take the climbers' path up talus into the basin below the west face. The route starts on a bolted face about 20 ft downhill of the large chockstone-filled chimney, just left of the Northwest Face's first pitch, and its top pitches finish up the Southwest Rib to the summit.
wa_morning_star_peak_standard: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east past the Verlot Public Service Center for about 17 miles, then turn right (south) onto Sunrise Mine Road, FS Road 4065, and follow it 2.2 miles to the trailhead at its end, at about 2,340 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Leave the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile in, just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, for a faint path up the river's east side past a house-sized boulder to the basin near 3,700 ft. Climb the steep gully directly east, then snowy slabs to the 5,600 ft notch in the southeast ridge; drop into the southeast basin, traverse right below the cliffs, climb the first broad gully to the south ridge and follow it north to the summit.
wa_mount_arriva_scramble: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway, about 45 miles east of Marblemount to the signed Easy Pass Trailhead pullout on the south side of the highway between mileposts 151 and 152, at about 3,700 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and camping beyond the pass inside the national park requires a backcountry permit. The highway is closed in winter.
About 300 yards from the trailhead, cross Granite Creek on a footlog, then climb the Easy Pass Trail through hemlock and fir forest to this crossing of Easy Pass Creek.

Keep climbing as the trail leaves the forest for the avalanche paths on the flanks of Ragged Ridge, crossing Easy Pass Creek and traversing steep rock slopes and avalanche meadows to the pass at about 6,500 ft.
Cross the pass into North Cascades National Park and descend its west side into the open meadows of Fisher Creek Basin below Arriva.

From the notch, scramble good rock along the south ridge crest until the summit block bars the way. Look for a narrow defile where a dark, eroded dike splits the block, climb it until a sloping ramp lets you traverse left back onto the crest, and scramble the crest to the top. If the block above is uniform pale rock with no dark band, you are not at the defile.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_glacier: From Sedro-Woolley, drive SR 20 east about 16 miles to milepost 82 and turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS 11). Continue about 18 miles; just past Boulder Creek Campground and the Boulder Creek bridge, turn left on FS 1130 for about 1 mile, then left on FS 1131 to the road end and the Boulder Ridge Trailhead (Trail #605) at about 2,700 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow Boulder Ridge Trail #605 about 2 nearly flat miles to a boggy clearing at the wilderness boundary, then a steep, unmaintained boot path up heather over a Class 3 rock band near 4,700 ft. Stay on the moraine crest north of Boulder Creek to camp where the ridge meets the ice, then rope up and climb the glacier west, south of the cleaver; skirt the big buttress near 9,500 ft to the south, cross the bergschrund and finish up steep snow to Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver: Follow Boulder Ridge Trail #605 about 2 flat miles to the boggy clearing at the wilderness boundary, then the user path up steep heather and a Class 3 rock step to camp where the ridge meets snow. Rope up and cross the lower glacier northwest to the toe of the cleaver near 6,800 ft, follow the cleaver, mostly on its north side, to the large rock buttress near 9,300 ft, then take one of the finishes past the buttress onto the summit plateau and Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge: Follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope Creeks (lowest early in the day), to the signed fork at about 2 miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier.

Rope up and head east-northeast across the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier, two to three hours through a crevasse field with thin snow bridges, then take low-to-moderate snow ramps to the foot of the ridge at about 7,500 to 7,800 ft on the east edge of the Roosevelt.

Climb the lower ridge on moderate snow, passing a pinnacle on its right and keeping to snow over the poor rock. Get around the junky towers and bergschrunds on the left (east) on ramps through the icefall, including a long contour east near 9,000 ft around a schrund, to the foot of the 300 ft Cockscomb Tower.

Pass the tower on its left (east) side by steep snow; late in the season, when that snow is gone, drop onto the Park Glacier and climb its AI3 headwall instead. Regain the crest above the tower, follow it as it broadens into the summit plateau, and cross the plateau to Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_coleman_deming: Follow Trail 677 as it switchbacks through old growth and avalanche chutes, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope Creeks (cross early, before afternoon melt). At the signed fork at about 2 miles go right on the climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft.

Rope up where the moraine meets the Coleman Glacier and climb south, then southeast toward the Black Buttes, weaving through crevasses. Higher, the track swings east beneath Colfax Peak; cross under its icefall without stopping, keeping off the avalanche-prone Colfax flank, to the broad saddle between Colfax and the summit cone at about 9,000 ft.

From the saddle turn east and climb about 300 ft up the pumice ridge on a boot path, then the steep snow of the Roman Wall to the right of its rock, roughly 9,300 to 10,400 ft. Where it eases onto the flat summit plateau, walk about ten minutes to Grant Peak; wand the top of the wall for the way back.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier: Take Park Butte Trail 603 across Sulphur Creek (a footbridge or logs, a ford at peak melt) and up through the meadow and forest switchbacks to Morovitz Meadow, the last running water. At the signed junction there go right on Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, up stone steps onto the moraine crest, and follow it with the Easton Glacier dropping away on your right to Sandy Camp, where the crest runs out near 5,900 ft.

Rope up at the glacier edge and climb roughly north toward Sherman Peak, keeping climber's right of the main crevasse bands. Near 9,400 to 9,700 ft at the rim of Sherman Crater, cross the rockfall-swept slope quickly and trend west across the saddle to the foot of the Roman Wall, climb its 35 to 45 degree snow staying right of the rocky rib, then cross the summit plateau to Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge: From the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542), continue about 1 mile east of the Glacier Public Service Center and turn right onto Glacier Creek Road (FS 39). Drive about 8 miles, turn left at a junction and continue less than half a mile to the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead for Trail 677, at about 3,700 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing Grouse, Kulshan and Heliotrope Creeks (lowest early in the day), to the signed fork at about 2.25 miles. Go right on the climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps around 6,000 ft at the edge of the Coleman Glacier.

Rope up and cross the Coleman Glacier east (climber's left) toward the toe of the North Ridge, threading seracs and open crevasses; the route changes yearly and often has no track. Arrive at the double bergschrund guarding the base of the ridge, and probe as you near it for a hidden third crack between the two visible ones.

Cross the double bergschrund on a bridge or narrow ramp and climb the broad 40 degree snow gully to the ridge crest. Follow the crest to the ice cliff near 9,600 ft and climb its steep ice, short near-vertical steps then sustained 60 to 65 degree ice, for several pitches. Above it the angle eases; trend climber's left through crevasses on the upper ice cap to the summit plateau and Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall: From I-5 Exit 255 in Bellingham, follow the Mount Baker Highway (WA-542) east through Glacier and past the Heather Meadows ski area to the road end at Artist Point, about 58 miles. The final stretch is usually snow-free only from about mid-July into early fall. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow the Chain Lakes Trail about a mile to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction, then the Ptarmigan Ridge Trail west along the crest past Coleman Pinnacle and Camp Kiser to the Portals, where most parties camp. Drop onto the Rainbow Glacier, cross onto the Park Glacier, and climb the headwall beneath the Cockscomb, crossing the bergschrund near 9,500 ft, to the summit plateau and Grant Peak.
wa_mount_baker_squak_glacier: From WA-20 at milepost 82, turn north onto Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive 12.5 miles to just past the Rocky Creek bridge. Turn left on FS Road 12 for 3.6 miles, then stay right on FS Road 13 for 5.3 miles to its end at the Schriebers Meadow (Park Butte) trailhead, about 3,360 ft. Road 13 is potholed and rocky; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.
wa_mount_blum_north_ridge: Drive Baker Lake Road (Forest Road 11) north from WA-20 at milepost 82, near Concrete, about 25.5 miles to its end at the Baker River Trailhead, about 774 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required.

Hike the Baker River Trail #606 about half a mile to the suspension bridge, cross it, and follow the trail downstream about 175 yards to an unmarked climbers' path just before the stringer bridge over Blum Creek. The faint path climbs steeply along Blum Creek's north bank and up Blum Creek Ridge, contouring its south side around 5,100 ft through huckleberry and talus into the Blum Lakes basin.

Continue past the lakes to the northernmost one, then cross the northwest shoulder into the glacial basin below the North Ridge and rope up to cross it. Cross the moat by a chockstone-filled gully, climb several sustained pitches on compact granite to gain the crest, and follow the serrated, easier ridge to the summit.
wa_mount_blum_south_ridge: Hike the Baker River Trail #606 about half a mile, roughly ten minutes, to the suspension bridge over the Baker River.

Cross the suspension bridge and follow the trail downstream along the far bank about 175 yards. The unmarked climbers' path leaves the trail about 25 yards before the stringer bridge over Blum Creek and heads up the creek's north bank.

Follow the faint path up Blum Creek's north bank through dense forest and devil's club; if you lose it, angle southeast to regain it near the creek. It then veers away from the creek and climbs the steep shoulder of Blum Creek Ridge to a narrow rock rib near 3,300 ft.
Keep climbing the steep, brushy crest of Blum Creek Ridge on faint tread through old growth and huckleberry until the path begins an ascending traverse along the south side of the ridge crests.
Continue the traverse along the ridge's south side through huckleberry brush and talus, then drop easily into the Blum Lakes basin. The usual camp is at the outlet of the middle lake.

Climb the class 3 sandy gully above the lakes to the upper lake at about 5,700 ft, work around the lake, and head into the snow couloir that climbs toward the bowl below the south ridge. Carry an ice axe; the snow can be firm early in the season.

Climb the couloir and granite slabs to gain the south ridge, then follow blocky class 3 scrambling along the south and southeast ridge to the broad summit plateau and the large cairn on the true summit. A grassy ledge right of the upper snowfield gives an easier finish.
wa_mount_chaval_scramble: Take the unsigned fisherman's path from the road and follow it upstream along the south side of Illabot Creek through old growth for about a mile, then turn uphill near the first major side creek, which can be a wet ford early in the season. Angle southeast and uphill around a belt of slide alder to the band of cliffs and gullies at about 4,000 to 4,300 ft; cairns and flagging are sparse here and it is easy to commit to the wrong gully.
wa_mount_custer_standard: Walk, or with a high-clearance 4WD vehicle drive, up the unsigned Depot Creek Road to the major washout where the track ends. Foot travel continues from here on the old logging-road grade.
Continue on foot along the old road grade, then follow the way trail into old-growth forest to the international boundary obelisk (Monument 65) and the North Cascades National Park register.

Follow the faint Depot Creek climbers' path up the valley, roughly 3 miles through timber and brush with no consistent tread, to the headwall where Depot Creek Falls drops. Cross the base of the falls on the fixed handlines over wet, slippery slabs; do not attempt it without them when the rock is wet.

Above the falls, climb the steep path onto the outwash plain and continue through scrub, talus and cobbles in the open basin below Mount Redoubt to Ouzel Lake, with camps on flat sandy benches near the lake.

From camp, scramble the large broken buttress southwest of the lake on cairned slabs, traverse far climber's right partway up, and continue onto the Redoubt Glacier. Cross the glacier, roped where crevasses warrant, to the low point of about 7,800 ft in the rock flying buttress toward Custer and Spickard.

Continue into the southwest basin below Custer's summit and climb toward the notch immediately south of the true summit at about 8,260 ft. The break through it is a vertical rock gully only 6 to 8 ft wide, sometimes holding ice, and pulling through it is the technical crux.
Above the gully, follow the loose, rust-coloured South Ridge the short remaining distance to the summit. The rock is extremely poor, so wear a helmet and test every hold.
wa_mount_despair_east_route: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 11 miles and turn left onto Thornton Lakes Road between mileposts 117 and 118. Follow this rough gravel road about 5 miles to its end at about 2,500 ft; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.
wa_mount_fury_east_mongo_ridge: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking lot near milepost 134, about 14 miles east of Newhalem, at roughly 2,100 ft. The trail drops about a mile to Ross Lake, where the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver Landing must be reserved in advance, and overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.
wa_mount_fury_east_southeast_glaciers: Follow the Ross Dam Trail down through forest about a mile to the gravel service road and turn right toward the lake; turning left crosses the dam and adds a long detour. Before the shore, a post marked Resort Phone on the left leads to the phone box: call the resort and wait at the shuttle dock for the reserved water taxi, or launch a canoe or packraft here.
Ride the water taxi, or paddle, about 4.6 miles north up Ross Lake to Big Beaver Landing at the mouth of Big Beaver Creek on the west shore, where the Big Beaver Creek Trail begins.

Follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail up the valley through groves of old-growth redcedar. The trail is well graded and largely flat, and Luna Camp, an established backcountry camp beside the creek, is reached after roughly 4 to 5 hours.

Continue up the Big Beaver Creek Trail about a mile, roughly half an hour, past Luna Camp, then leave the trail on the unmaintained, flagged climbers' path and cross Big Beaver Creek toward Access Creek. There is no bridge, so cross on a log or expect a cold ford that can run thigh-deep.

Bushwhack up the Access Creek drainage for about a mile: devil's club in the valley bottom, a crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where the brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry brush and a final half-mile of talus into the basin at about 4,300 ft.

From the basin, climb the long, steep, loose scree chute about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, which can be hot with no shade. From the col, traverse steep heather and talus to Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep heather sections.

Skirt the knob above Luna Pass on a broad ledge on its northwest side and follow the Northeast Ridge over its ups and downs, including a 25-ft Class 3 crack. Where the crest drops away, descend a narrow heather chute about 500 ft, contour southwest to a rocky rib and take its lower ledge, then rope up for the right side of the Southeast Glacier, passing a bergschrund near 7,900 ft and climbing snow to nearly 50 degrees to the summit.
wa_mount_goode_northeast_buttress: Drive SR-20 to the Bridge Creek Trailhead at about milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass; the lot is on the north side of the highway, and a short connector trail across the road joins the Pacific Crest Trail southbound. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, and overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.
wa_mount_herman_standard_scramble: From I-5 Exit 255 in Bellingham, follow SR 542, the Mount Baker Highway, east about 56 miles through Glacier to the Heather Meadows area at the Mt. Baker Ski Area. Turn into the large parking lot signed for Bagley Lakes, at about 4,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park.
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to Colonial Creek Campground near milepost 130 on Diablo Lake. The Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground, near the boat ramp, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south along Thunder Arm and up the Thunder Creek valley, past McAllister and Tricouni camps, about 10 miles to Junction Camp at the Fisher Creek Trail junction. The last mile or so below the camp is a steep climb.

Stay on the Thunder Creek Trail rather than turning onto the Fisher Creek Trail, and continue up the upper Thunder Creek valley past Thunder Basin to Park Creek Pass, a broad, rocky trough at about 6,000 ft at the head of the creek.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and climb east about 500 ft into the moraine, then traverse north around a broad ridge over heather and rock for roughly 1.5 to 2 miles, crossing a rib near 7,600 ft and a gully through cliff bands that can hold snow or ice, to the bivy sites on the saddle at the southern edge of the Fremont Glacier.

Rope up and make the gentle glacier crossing north from camp to the Hogsback, the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier. Late in the season a bergschrund and a moat can open where the snow meets the rock.

Cross the moat onto rock and climb a Class 3-4 pitch to a left-slanting ramp, a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands, which leads up to the summit ridge. Do not head straight at the summit tower from the glacier.

Traverse exposed Class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge through the U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn, then climb a final Class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on solid rock to the tiny summit.
wa_mount_logan_r1: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to Colonial Creek Campground near milepost 130 on Diablo Lake. The Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

Take the Thunder Creek Trail about 10 miles to the Fisher Creek Trail, then Fisher Creek Trail about 3 miles to just past a handrailed log bridge, and climb that stream's drainage off-trail to a lake camp near 5,160 ft. Climb south-southeast to Christmas Tree Col, drop onto the Banded Glacier and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col, then gain the northeast ridge on rock near 8,800 ft and scramble the Class 3-4 summit block.
wa_mount_logan_r2: Hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.5 miles to Easy Pass, descend into Fisher Basin to the Fisher Creek valley floor, cross the creek on a large fallen log, and follow a faint path up the east side of the Douglas Creek valley through dense slide alder. Above the brush, climb a gully on the west side of the basin, with a short steep step, onto polished slabs and scramble about 1,500 ft up them to the toe of the glacier.
Ascend the Douglas Glacier, steep near its head, to the col, then traverse to meet the upper Banded Glacier and finish up the roughly 300-ft Class 3-4 summit block.
wa_mount_pilchuck_standard_route: From Granite Falls, follow the Mountain Loop Highway east about 10 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center. Continue about 1 mile, cross the South Fork Stillaguamish River, and turn right onto Mount Pilchuck Road, FS Road 42. Drive about 6.8 miles, mostly rough gravel with a paved final stretch, to the road-end trailhead at about 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park.

Follow the Mount Pilchuck Trail #700 through old-growth forest and subalpine meadow about 2 miles to the open boulder field below the summit, then follow the orange blazes painted on the rocks across it. Scramble 20 to 30 ft up the summit block and climb the short fixed ladder onto the lookout deck. Do not shortcut into the old ski-area clearing west of the trail.
wa_mount_prophet_east: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking lot near milepost 134, a few miles east of Diablo. Overnight stays need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

Descend the trail steeply about 0.8 mile to a gravel service road, go left briefly, then turn right down to Ross Dam. Cross the dam and follow the trail north along the west shore of Ross Lake about 6 miles to Big Beaver Creek and the Big Beaver Trail junction. A water taxi to Big Beaver Landing skips this shoreline stretch.

Turn west up the Big Beaver Trail and follow it about 5 miles up the valley through old-growth forest to Thirtynine Mile Creek and its camp, the last reliable water and last legal campsite before leaving the trail.
Leave the Big Beaver Trail between the Thirtynine Mile Creek crossing and the camp marker post, heading north into a brushy gully.
Climb north up the brushy gully and the rib beside it, a hard bushwhack through steep timber and brush where most of the day's gain happens, until you break out on the crest of Thirtynine Mile Ridge.
Follow the crest north through open forest and then open walking to the saddle at about 6,600 ft where the rib meets the south ridge. There is no water here; carry it up from Thirtynine Mile Creek.
Follow the crest north at Class 1-2 over the rounded Point 6690 to the rocky Point 7361 and on to Point 7547, the top of the north-south ridgeline. Watch for cornices early in the season.
Point 7547 is a false summit. Turn west a short distance from it; the last few feet to the true summit are a short, steep Class 3 scramble with moderate exposure.
wa_mount_prophet_southwest_rib: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east into North Cascades National Park to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking area near milepost 134. A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay, including the camp in the Big Beaver valley.

Descend the Ross Dam Trail about 0.8 mile, cross Ross Dam and follow the Big Beaver Trail north along Ross Lake (or take the water taxi to Big Beaver Landing), then up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp. Climb the forested rib, traverse southeast past the short Class 4 ledge near 5,450 ft, bypass the 6,900 ft cliff band by the snow ramp on its right, and follow the crest from the 7,420 ft saddle, passing a gendarme on its south side.
wa_mount_pugh_pika_slab: Follow Mt. Pugh Trail #644 about 1.5 miles up through mature forest, with a few stream crossings, to Lake Metan near 3,200 ft. Fill up here; there is no reliable water higher on the mountain.

Round the north side of the lake, then switchback hard up steep forested slopes, breaking out into an open boulder-strewn basin near 4,900 ft, and continue up to the notch of Stujack Pass at about 5,700 ft, where the maintained trail ends.
wa_mount_pugh_stujack: Follow Trail #644 about 1.5 miles through old-growth forest, with several stream crossings and about 1,300 ft of gain, to Lake Metan. It is the last reliable water on the route.

Round the north side of the lake and switchback steeply up through forest, then talus and meadows past an open boulder basin near 4,900 ft, to the notch of Stujack Pass at about 5,700 ft, where the maintained trail ends. Snow often lingers on this stretch into midsummer.

Climb left out of the notch on heather, contour the east side of the ridge and cross the head of a small permanent snowfield, then follow the knife-edge crest on chipped, blasted ledges past the short Class 3 chimney with an iron ring. Ignore stray cairns that lead toward the cliff edge. The true high point is a roughly 10 ft boulder at the edge of the flat summit plateau.
wa_mount_saul_se_route: Follow Indian Creek Trail #1502 from the road end about 0.3 mile to the footbridge over the glacier-fed White River. The bridge has washed out in the past; if it is gone, the river must be forded, which is easiest in the morning.

Continue up the Indian Creek valley on the mostly flat trail through old growth and stretches of burned forest for about 4 miles to near Airplane Creek, where you leave the maintained trail. Nothing marks the departure.

Climb steeply north up the Airplane Creek drainage through devil's club, vine maple, blowdown and burned standing timber; keeping to the drainage about a quarter mile downstream of Airplane Creek avoids the worst of the brush. In early season snow begins around 4,000 ft.

Keep climbing the drainage, on continuous snow above about 4,700 ft in early season, to Airplane Lake at about 5,280 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the trail. The flat peninsula on the north side of the lake is the usual camp.
Boulder-hop across the lake's outlet and head west up open slopes toward the low point on the ridge east of the summit, to the foot of the upper east face at about 6,200 ft.

Choose a line by snow cover; the direct ascent of the clean, continuous east-face slabs is the one to aim for, and on a snowy year it is a snow climb wanting an axe. Finish with a short, exposed Class 3 scramble to the broad, rocky summit; the register sits among rocks about 15 ft below and west of the true high point.
wa_mount_sefrit_bloody_head_couloir: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 13 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32). Follow it about 5.3 miles to its end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead beside Hannegan Campground, at about 3,120 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge: Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead (there is no bridge; wade it or use a downed log if one is present), then follow the old logging roadbed of Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for about 50 minutes to around 2,700 ft, where you leave the trail.

Leave the roadbed and start an unmarked ascending traverse up steep forest toward Sefrit's southwest ridge, through slide alder, old avalanche debris and rotten downed timber. There is no path, and route-finding is the main time sink of the day.
Keep traversing upward, passing through or around the cliff band, until the brush gives way to subalpine meadows on the ridge near 5,800 ft.

Cross the meadows east to the summit gully system above the cliff band. Where it forks, take the leftmost fork, the rock fork just west of a snow couloir on its right; the rock is solid low and loosens higher up.
Climb the loose, blocky Class 4 gully through the final rock band onto the summit ridge and follow it a short way east to the broad, rocky summit.
