wa_mount_shuksan_northwest_arete: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 18 miles to the hairpin switchback at roughly 3,500 ft, about a quarter mile below the ski area's White Salmon Day Lodge, and turn onto White Salmon Road (FS 3075). Parking is very limited and is not allowed on the highway shoulder; do not block the gate. No parking pass is required.

Follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile, then drop off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climb to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area. Follow that crest to the base of the mountain's north side and gain the northwest arete, a long line of loose, runout rock, moderate ice and glacier travel, to the summit.
wa_mount_shuksan_sulphide_glacier: Follow Shannon Ridge Trail #742, an old roadbed heading northeast, for about 2 miles to where the road tread ends near 3,800 ft, weaving through a belt of blowdown. Continue on true trail angling left through brush onto the open ridge crest and up to timberline near 4,600 ft, where snow often lingers into midsummer.
wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 18 miles to the hairpin switchback at roughly 3,500 ft, below the ski area, and park in the small pull-off at the gated White Salmon Road (FS 3075). Parking is very limited and is not allowed on the highway shoulder; do not block the gate. No parking pass is required.
wa_mount_stickney_scramble: Walk the closed Olney Creek logging road uphill about 2.25 miles, past a first switchback, to a second switchback where the grade eases around 3,700 ft. Nothing is signed here and mapped road alignments are unreliable, so go by the switchback on the ground.
Leave the road on the unsigned but well-established boot path on the right (north) side, which climbs onto a forested ridge crest and follows it until the tread fades out around 4,050 to 4,200 ft.

Leave the tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake.
Pass the lake on its east side and follow the drainage above it up to a cluster of small tarns around 4,500 ft.

Work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block, into the rocky basin and boulder field below it. The gully to take is the one on the right, immediately west of the summit hump; in winter and spring at least one avalanche-prone slope is crossed on the way.
Climb the wet, loose, easy fourth-class gully to the notch just under the summit ridge, then walk and scoot across the short, exposed ridge past a small plateau to the final rock hump.
wa_mount_terror_north_face: Follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek on a gentle grade to a stone cairn and arrow near 1,700 ft that marks the unsigned start of the Terror Basin climbers' path. A small campsite sits here, and the spot is easy to walk past in fog.

Take the hard right at the cairn rather than continuing straight on the fainter track along Terror Creek, and climb the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path directly up through old-growth forest, over 3,000 ft in about 1.5 miles, until it breaks out above treeline around 5,000 ft.

Above the trees, make a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields to the broad saddle and rock notch near 6,200 ft overlooking Terror Basin. Expect loose rock and some route-finding on the upper slabs.
Drop about 400 ft beyond the saddle into the gravelly, flower-filled basin at about 5,800 ft, where several small streams give reliable water.

Cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, then cross the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descend the crevassed Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque to the foot of the face. Start just left of the snowpatch, climb long rightward-traversing third-class ground onto the right (west) rib, follow dihedrals to the darkening west crest, then move back left onto the face to the chimney.

Above the chimney, follow the long snow finger up the upper face, scramble the wildly exposed crest, and traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. Take the false summit on an exposed easy fifth-class hand traverse, downclimb it, and make the short climb to the true summit.
wa_mount_terror_southeast_face: Turn north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground onto the unpaved Goodell Creek Road and follow it to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay; this cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Follow the old roadbed along Goodell Creek about 4 miles, then the steep cairned climbers' path up to camp in Terror Basin around 5,800 ft. Cross the Barrier at the roughly 6,400 ft Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin, ascend slabs and talus on the east side to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle, and climb the short, steep four-pitch ridge above it to the summit.
wa_mount_terror_stoddard_buttress: Turn north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground onto the unpaved Goodell Creek Road and follow it to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay; this cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Hike from Goodell Creek to high camp in Crescent Creek Basin, about 6,000 ft of gain. On the climbing day cross the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descend the Mustard Glacier to the base of the north face, then scramble onto the buttress crest, simul-climb long stretches of low fifth class along it, and finish on two exposed knife-edge pitches and a sharp prow, the 5.8 crux, to the summit.
wa_mount_terror_west_ridge: Turn north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground onto the unpaved Goodell Creek Road and follow it to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay; this cross-country zone is walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Follow the old roadbed along Goodell Creek about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb the steep, pink-flagged climbers' track past moss-covered cliffs into Crescent Creek Basin, nearly 6,000 ft of gain to camp. From the basin climb the narrow, loose west gully to the chockstone notch between Terror and The Rake, then about 100 ft of low fifth-class crack and 250 ft of class 3 to the summit.
wa_mount_torment_south_ridge: Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then turn sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. It switchbacks up through forest across four small creeks to treeline and the low camps around 5,300 ft, then continues up open slabs and tundra on the skier's right of Boston Creek to high camp near 6,200 to 6,400 ft.

Leave the trail and make a rising traverse northwest near the 6,200 ft contour beneath Forbidden Peak's south spur, crossing a prominent rock rib below the cliffs. Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's left and follow it up to the deep couloir breaking the rock band on the left; cross the bergschrund or moat and scramble about 100 ft of loose class 3-4 to the notch.

Climb an open book angling left off the notch, turn right at its top to a ledge, and take a short second open book to the crest. Pass a steeper tower on sloping, exposed ledges, weave among towers continuing leftward on the southwest face, and finish on sustained fourth and low fifth-class granite to the summit.
wa_mount_torment_torment_forbidden_trave: Follow the old mining road about three quarters of a mile to the old mine site, then take the sharp right onto the steep, unmaintained climbers' trail. It switchbacks up through forest with four creek crossings to treeline around 5,300 ft, then eases across heather benches and talus into Boston Basin, with high camp at roughly 6,200 to 6,400 ft.

Traverse northwest across the upper basin to the toe of the Taboo Glacier, rope up, and climb it and the east couloir past the moat to the notch at the base of Torment's South Ridge. Climb the ridge to Torment's summit, rappel from the notch onto the Forbidden Glacier, cross it to the saddle, and follow the Sidewalk in the Sky crest to the West Ridge Notch and up Forbidden's West Ridge to the summit.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 11 miles and turn left onto Thornton Lakes Road between mileposts 117 and 118, just west of Newhalem. Follow this rough gravel road about 5 miles to the trailhead at road's end, around 2,700 ft; high clearance is recommended.

Hike the Thornton Lakes Trail to the ridge above the lakes and drop to the lake outlet. Follow the climbers' path past the middle lake, then climb a long, loose scree and talus gully northwest to the bivy col at about 5,800 ft. From the col, cross the glacier remnant on the east flank to the low notch in the Northeast Ridge, gain it by the ramp on its right, and follow the ridge to the summit.
wa_mount_watson_scramble: Follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 from the lot through forest for about a mile to the meadow junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1.
Stay right on Trail #611 toward the lakes rather than climbing left toward the old Anderson Butte lookout site, and continue to the next junction at about 4,700 ft.
Take the left fork, which climbs about half a mile to a small saddle at the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness boundary; the right fork drops to lower Anderson Lake.
Follow the trail down off the saddle to the Watson Lakes at about 4,400 ft. The maintained trail ends here, and the lakes are the last reliable water.
Leave the tread at the lakes and follow the open, cairned climbers' route up talus, heather and, into summer, snow on the slopes below the peak to the bivy sites around 5,400 ft.

Climb the widest gully east of the peak to the saddle at about 5,900 ft, avoiding the west gully. From the saddle, head west along the south side of the ridge into the basin below the summit block, cross it to the heather-and-dirt gully on the block's south side, squeeze through the trees partway up, then scramble the short block and the narrow, exposed 30 ft ridge to the top.
wa_narcos: From the lot, walk up through the woods toward the wall on an unmaintained, intermittently cairned climbers' line, gaining elevation quickly, then traverse left through open forest and across slabby benches to a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.
wa_neve_glacier_west_ridge: From Newhalem, drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) east past Gorge Lake to the Pyramid Lake Trailhead at milepost 126.8. Park in the small lot on the north side of the highway; the signed trail starts across the road beside Pyramid Creek. No parking pass is needed, but overnight stays in the backcountry require a North Cascades National Park Complex backcountry permit.

Hike the Pyramid Lake Trail 2.1 miles to Pyramid Lake (no camping there), then take the steep, brushy climbers' path from the lake onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge and south to camps by the Colonial Glacier moraine. Climb the Colonial Glacier to the col near 6,800 ft, drop onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped to the northwest-facing gully that gains the west ridge, then scramble class 3-4 past a notch to the summit.
wa_news_nw_corner: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 30 miles, over Washington Pass, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway about a mile west of the pass, at roughly 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or day-use fee is required to park. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, so there is no drive-up access until it reopens in spring.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the signed climbing-access junction just past a small stream (the last water), then take the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces and traverse north along the base to a corner and crack leading to a treed ledge. Five pitches of 5.8-5.9 corners, wide cracks and an offwidth finish left around a roof to the summit.
wa_nooksack_tower_beckey_route: Cross Ruth Creek on a log or by wading at the trailhead, then follow the old roadbed about 2 miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead near 2,550 ft. From there, watch for a flagged, easy-to-miss spot where the climbers' route leaves the trail and drops steeply to the Nooksack River.

Ford the Nooksack on a log if one is in place (they are swept away and replaced most years), then climb the steep forested slope toward Price Lake, starting up the west bank of Price Creek until a sound log lets you cross it, and continue to the lake at about 3,900 ft.
From the lake, climb onto the moraine above it and follow the crest of the rib upward on a faint goat path to flat rock slabs at about 5,900 ft, the last good bivy before the tower.

Rope up and get onto the glacier, traverse climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the tower, then descend from it onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier and cross the crevassed lower glacier toward the tower's base. Losing height off the saddle is correct.

Cross the bergschrund at about 6,500 ft at the foot of the north face (when it is hollow, parties swing wide left) and climb into the couloir above it on 50-degree snow and ice, early in the day before the sun starts rockfall.
wa_nooksack_tower_south_face: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 12.5 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32). In just over a mile turn right onto Nooksack Cirque Road (FS 34) and follow it about a mile to the parking area at the road end by Ruth Creek, about 2,150 ft. No parking pass is needed; overnight stays require a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.

Follow the North Face approach: cross Ruth Creek, walk the old roadbed about 2 miles, ford the Nooksack, and climb past Price Lake onto the moraine and rib above it. At the top of the rib, traverse onto the East Nooksack Glacier rather than the Price and climb it to where the south face rises straight out of the ice; the route starts on the face's right side and runs about 12 pitches to the summit.
wa_north_face_3: Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail through forest about 1.5 to 2 miles, until the terrain opens up, to where a well-worn climbers' path branches off uphill to the left at a large cairn. The junction is easy to miss.

Take the climbers' path as it steepens, switchbacking through heather and larch onto talus below Concord and Lexington Towers, and aim for the gully that separates those two towers rather than the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.
Zig-zag up the loose scree and talus of the gully to the broad notch between Concord and Lexington Towers. The upper gully often holds firm snow into early summer, when an axe or traction is useful.

From the col, move slightly west and drop a couple of feet to a right-leaning crack on the Lexington side. Pitch 1 starts with the awkward 5.7 crux and eases into 5.6 chimney stemming to a large belay block; pitch 2 wanders right over blocky, mossy ground to the notch between the true and west summits.
Scramble or lead the exposed, knobby 'Stegosaur' ridge crest from the notch to the true summit; many parties unrope here.
wa_north_face_var_right_directisimo: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 30 miles, over Washington Pass, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway about a mile west of the pass, at roughly 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or day-use fee is required to park. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, so there is no drive-up access until it reopens in spring.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, take the climbers' path that breaks off just past a small stream up slabs and talus, bear left where it splits, and climb the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. Climb the North Face's first pitch to a treed ledge, then the steeper direct crack line right of the standard route, and easy low-fifth ground up and left to the summit.
wa_north_ridge_2: Hike Trail #674 about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side past Boundary Camp into the Chilliwack River valley. Follow the rough Chilliwack River Trail down-valley past Copper Creek and US Cabin camps, cross the river by the hand-operated cable car or a ford, and at the Brush Creek Trail junction near mile 12 turn up Brush Creek past Graybeal and Whatcom camps to the pass, about 16 miles in all.

From the pass, leave the maintained trail on a faint climbers' path heading directly south onto the broad toe of the north ridge. When the path gives out on snow patches and broken rock, stay on or near the crest; the final 400 ft to the summit is loose, very exposed Class 3.
wa_north_ridge_4: Drive SR 20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to Colonial Creek Campground on Diablo Lake's Thunder Arm, just past milepost 130, and turn into the south loop. Park in the lot above the boat ramp; the Thunder Creek Trail starts at the south end of the campground near the amphitheater, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays need a North Cascades wilderness permit.
wa_north_ridge_7: From SR 20 in Marblemount, cross the Skagit River onto Cascade River Road and follow it, paved and then gravel, about 22 miles to a small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg Mountain, just below the road end at Cascade Pass. The unmaintained Boston Basin climbers' path leaves here along the old Diamond Mine roadbed. Overnight stays in Boston Basin need a North Cascades wilderness permit.
wa_north_ridge_west_side: Drive SR 20 to Rainy Pass, about 37 miles east of Newhalem, and turn onto the short access road on the north side of the highway to the PCT north trailhead lot at about 4,860 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or day-use fee is required to park.

Follow the PCT north about 1.5 miles to just before the Porcupine Creek bridge, near 5,250 ft, then leave the trail and climb the ridge northeast about 2 miles and 2,300 ft to the base of the North Ridge; the second gully is the cleaner line. Climb the west rib and the steeper upper pitches of coarse, vertically jointed granite to the summit.
wa_north_twin_sister_scramble: Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and climb the graded logging road, which most parties ride on mountain bikes. At the first major fork, about 2.5 miles up, stay right; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after a second, sturdier bridge, take the left fork and continue to around mile 5, where the road ends near a dirt mound and cairn.

Leave the road for an old, overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut, where brush soaks clothing even on a dry day and there is no tread or cairns to follow in fog. Around mile 6.4 you reach the old fire ring.

Start the headwall on its left and stay climber's left; ground that looks easier to the right turns into loose, exposed Class 4-5. Climb straight over the false-summit crag on steep Class 3, then take the broken chimney or traverse right around a corner into a rock-and-gully system, scrambling Class 3-4 to the summit. Several false tops near the end are easy to mistake for it.
wa_north_twin_sister_west_ridge: From I-5 Exit 255 in Bellingham, take SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) east about 16.7 miles and turn right on Mosquito Lake Road. After about 4.8 miles, just south of Porter Creek, turn left onto Middle Fork Road (Road 38) and follow it about 4.8 miles, then turn right down to the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and park at the gate, about 1,200 ft. Beyond is private timberland; a landowner recreation permit is required.

Cross the bridge and bike or walk the gated logging roads toward Dailey Prairie, roughly 2,000 to 2,500 ft of gain, to the climbers' trail. Follow it up through clearcut and timber onto the West Ridge near treeline, then scramble the crest on solid, high-friction rock past occasional cairns, the Obelisk and the Cockscomb to the summit.
wa_northeast_face_direct: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto the Cascade River Road and follow it 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass trailhead, about 3,600 ft. The first third is paved and the rest is gravel, narrow and steep near the end; the upper road usually opens by late June or early July.

Take the trail to Cascade Pass, then leave it across the Mixup flank, climb the Cache Glacier to Cache Col and descend to Kool-Aid Lake. Continue south across the Red Ledge, drop several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier, and cross to the Formidable Glacier. Climb it on its northern side, cross the moat into the hidden couloir, and follow the face to the north ridge and summit.
wa_northeast_ridge_1963_route: Walk a short way back down the road from the parking lot, descend the dirt embankment, and ford the infant Cascade River below the terminal moraine. The crossing runs higher as the day warms.
wa_northwest_buttress: Follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 up the creek through old growth until the maintained tread ends at a washout below the West Face basin. Scramble the washout to the cairned exit, usually flagged pink, where the climbers' path leaves left around 3,500 ft.

Climb the path steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench to the Bedal-Sloan saddle, and stay in the meadows below the West Face rather than heading toward the glacier. Start on the corner of darker rock at the lowest, leftmost point of the face, climb nine pitches up the buttress, exit by a short hand crack, and scramble third and fourth class to the sub-summit and summit.
wa_northwest_face_2: Drive SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) east past Washington Pass and park in the large pullout at the first big hairpin switchback, about a mile east of the pass near 5,100 ft. This is the same pullout used for the Hairpin Crags and Spire Gully. The highway closes over the pass in winter.

Take the climbers' trail south across the boulder field and up through forest and talus to Kangaroo Pass. Contour left below the slabs off Wallaby Peak to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger and climb it toward the notch, branching right onto the bench trail about 200 ft below the notch to the base of the face. Climb five pitches to the summit block.
wa_northwest_face_boving_pollock: The Blue Lake Trailhead is on the south side of SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) a little under a mile west of Washington Pass, between mileposts 161 and 162, about 42 miles east of Newhalem or 31 miles west of Winthrop. The paved lot is small and fills early. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required.

Follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1 to 1.25 miles to the clearing on the spire's northwest side, then take the climbers' path up talus and heather into the basin below the northwest face. Find the chockstone-filled chimney between the two formations; the route starts at the steep corner entered by a traverse, just right of the bolted Mojo Rising start. Climb six pitches to the summit.
wa_northwest_mox_peak_standard: From Trans-Canada Highway 1 Exit 119 in Chilliwack, BC, head south through Sardis and turn left onto Chilliwack Lake Road just before the river bridge. Follow it about 32 miles, past Chilliwack Lake, to the narrow, unsigned Depot Creek Road on the left near the lake's south end. High-clearance 4WD can go about 2.5 miles; park near 2,350 ft where the road becomes impassable. Carry a passport for the border.

Walk the old logging road about 2 miles to the US border and trail start, which climbs steeply to Depot Creek Falls; a climbers' path with fixed ropes passes the falls to Lake Ouzel (5,700 ft). Scramble the broken buttress southwest of the lake onto the Redoubt Glacier, traverse WSW about 2 miles to a flat near 7,300 ft, then contour southeast and climb the wet headwall at the glacier's eastern edge onto the northeast ridge to the summit.
wa_northwest_ridge_2: Walk the old mining road about a mile to the old mine site, then climb the steep, eroded climbers' path through forest, crossing several streams, until it breaks out of the trees near 5,300 ft at the remains of an old mining cabin.

Continue up the path onto the open basin slopes to the last and largest creek crossing. If the direct crossing looks hard, follow a path along the edge of the ravine to an easier spot where it drops in to cross; fill water here.
Across the creek, the path climbs a short way to the lower camps on a moraine ridge with small trees, just below the bare slabs left by the receding Quien Sabe Glacier.
wa_nw_face_var_remsberg_variation: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the road about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park. The highway is closed through the winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it reopens.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow and take the climbers' path left past a small stream, up slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Leave the gully at its split about 200 ft below the notch and scramble a low fifth-class step onto the west-side bench to the start. Five pitches, the third via the Remsberg crack, reach the west summit; scramble down into the notch and up to the main summit.
wa_one_piece_at_a_time: Start on the Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the kiosk and follow it, or the old roadbed beside it, for the first few minutes, then turn uphill to the left into the forest. A climbers' path through brush, trees and talus trends right toward the buttress and reaches a flat area beneath the cliff, about 45 minutes to 2 hours. Not every cairn marks the way; navigate on the wall.
wa_ottohorn_southeast_route: Follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber and levels around 1,100 ft. Around mile 3.5, near 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream by a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path; this is the last reliable water for a long way.
From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then make a long rising traverse across the snow, slabs and talus of Crescent Creek Basin to the camp below Mount Terror and the Himmelhorn.

Continue the rising traverse of the basin toward the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and crampon up the final snow and scree pitch to the col. Late season it is loose class 3-4 scrambling, and an overhanging boulder near the top is bypassed on its left. Note where you cross the moat for the way down.

From the col, scramble the east ridge, mostly class 3, to the summit, roughly an hour round trip. A rockfall scar about 30 ft below the summit ridge has forced at least one party to rope up for about two pitches of 5.7, so look at the last 100 ft before committing.
wa_painted_traverse: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 16 miles and turn left (east) onto FS Road 49, the North Fork Sauk Road. Follow it about 6.4 miles to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead at the road end near 2,100 ft; the road is rough and a high-clearance vehicle helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

About 100 yards up the North Fork Sauk Trail, take the old lookout trail branching left and switchback about a mile through forest to the old lookout site near 3,100 ft. Above it a steep, unmaintained climbers' path goes almost straight uphill, over a short cliff band that needs class 3 scrambling, into meadows and up the south ridge to Painted Mountain's summit.

Descend Painted's northeast ridge to a saddle and continue over Magenta Peak. The row of gendarmes east of Magenta forces you off the crest onto steep heather, a mossy downclimb and loose gullies below it; keep heading east to Black Mountain and finish on its short, exposed class 3-4 summit block.
wa_phantom_peak_south_route: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 13 miles and turn left onto the Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32). At 1.3 miles stay left on the Ruth Creek road and drive about 4 more miles to the trailhead at the road end near 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
wa_plan_9_from_outer_space: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 13 miles to just past milepost 119. Immediately after crossing the Goodell Creek bridge, turn left and follow the gravel road past a gravel pit and up to its end at the Upper Goodell Group Camp. Park there; the unmarked climbers' path up Goodell Creek starts behind the camp. Overnight stays need a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
wa_playing_not_spraying: From Winthrop, drive SR-20 west about 18 miles and turn left onto FS Road 5310-200, between mileposts 176 and 175 and about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. Follow it to the parking by a gravel pit at the road end near 3,000 ft; the trail starts at the southeast end of the pit. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required.

Walk the Cedar Creek Trail west about 5 miles, then turn off to the right below the old burn and follow a rough path up the right-hand side of the creek that drains the Silver Horn's south side to meadows near 6,200 ft. From the foot of the clean white south face, the route's eight pitches start on a large flake and finish through a deep chimney to the summit.
wa_poltergeist_pinnacle: Hike the Hannegan Pass Trail about 4 miles up the Ruth Creek valley, climbing steadily through forest and then open slopes to Hannegan Pass, where the trail crests.
Drop east from the pass on the trail a little under a mile to Boundary Camp at the head of the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down into the Chilliwack valley, cross the river, and climb onto Easy Ridge, following its long, partly brushy climbers' path east. Cross the Imperfect Impasse, a moat-and-cliff notch that often needs a short low fifth-class downclimb, climb snowfields to camp at Perfect Pass, then rope up and traverse east around the Challenger Arm onto the Challenger Glacier.

Continue roped across the upper glacier toward the cirque below the subsidiary summits, picking out the tower by the huge dark shield streaked with pale dikes at its base. The climb starts in a clean dihedral just left of the shield, about 20 ft above the bergschrund, and the East Face pitches lead to the top.
wa_primus_peak_south_ridge: From SR-20 in Marblemount, cross the Skagit River onto the Cascade River Road and drive about 20 miles, gravel after about mile 10, to the Eldorado climbers' parking near milepost 20 at about 2,100 ft. Overnight camps need a backcountry permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Cross the river on a log just downstream of the parking and climb the steep climbers' path and the boulder field near 4,000 ft into Eldorado Basin. Rope up and cross the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers north to Klawatti Col, pass the 50 ft notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, round Austera's east ridge onto the North Klawatti Glacier, and scramble talus up the south face to the summit.
wa_ptarmigan_traverse: Drive SR-20 to Marblemount and, where the highway turns left, keep straight onto Cascade River Road. Follow it about 23 miles, roughly an hour, to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (about 3,600 ft). No parking pass is needed; camping in the national park section of the traverse requires a backcountry permit from the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
Follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail up its long switchbacks about 3.7 miles to the broad saddle of Cascade Pass (5,392 ft). This is the last graded tread and the last easy water of the trip.

Do not follow the trail on east down toward Pelton Basin. Turn south at the pass, step off the tread onto heather and talus, and climb toward the apron of permanent snow under the ridge; rope up and ascend the Cache Glacier to the notch of Cache Col at its head, watching for a cornice on the lip.
From Cache Col, descend the snow and talus on the south side and traverse to Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first bivy at about 6,100 ft.
From Kool-Aid Lake, head south to the Red Ledges below Art's Knoll, a narrow, exposed class 3 ledge crossing on lichen-covered rock; it is especially treacherous when wet.
Beyond the ledges, get onto the Middle Cascade Glacier and climb it roped, through crevasses and past the bergschrund at its head, to Spider-Formidable Col.
From the col, descend the steep gullies and snow on the south side to the Yang Yang Lakes bivy.

From Yang Yang Lakes, climb onto the Le Conte Glacier and cross it roped, as it is often the most crevassed section of the traverse. Then descend steep gullies and snowfields to the South Cascade Glacier and follow it south to White Rock Lakes.

From the Itswoot Ridge camp, climb northeast onto the Dome Glacier and ascend it, about 35 degrees, to the summit ridge; a short exposed class 3 scramble along the knife-edged crest gains the summit. This is an optional side trip, and the traverse itself does not cross the peak.
wa_ragged_edge: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles and turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065), marked by small signs. Follow the gravel about 2.3 miles to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, around 2,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Take Sunrise Mine Trail #707, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs almost at once (harder in high runoff), then climb through Wirtz Basin and up cairned talus to the narrow, loose couloir of Headlee Pass, about 2.7 miles. Watch for rockfall from parties above.
From the pass, drop through trees and cross about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, then follow it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan). This is the last dependable water.
Continue on the Vesper summit path up talus and slabs to about 5,700 ft, to a saddle marked by two large cairns with Copper Lake visible below to the northwest. Do not drop into the saddle.

About 30 ft above the cairns, gain the heather ledge system on third-class slabs and follow its goat trail across the north face for roughly 800 ft until the ledge runs out. The common start is an exposed third-class traverse down and around the toe of a buttress to a clean 5.6 layback flake. The ledge holds snow and is treacherous when wet.
Climb the route's six pitches. The last is a long, easy, exposed romp up the arete that tops out on the summit.
wa_ragged_ridge: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur road signed for Easy Pass, which ends at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park, and camping on the national park side of the pass needs a backcountry permit.

Hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.4 miles and about 2,900 ft to Easy Pass, then descend the far side into the Fisher Creek basin at about 5,100 ft. Leave the trail and climb off-trail to a high camp at about 6,700 ft on Mesahchie's south shoulder, then ascend northwest to the Mesahchie-Katsuk saddle and scramble to the summit.
wa_rampage: From the pullout, go down the talus into the forest and cross Early Winters Creek on a log. Then climb the steep timbered rib on the north side of the creek draining Burgundy Col for about two hours, to the basin bench at roughly 6,500 ft. The spring here is the last reliable water.

Keep climbing the path toward Burgundy Col. Before topping out, cut right across a very loose slope onto a third-class ledge system, or go to the col and descend about 300 ft along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Walk the ledge right to its far end, where the big clean corner rises, and climb the route's four pitches.
wa_rapple_grapple: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the road, a little under a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook. The lot is small and fills early. A Northwest Forest Pass, interagency pass or day-use fee is required.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow. Take the climbers' path left past the small stream, up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, and stay right at the gully fork to reach the shared Beckey Route start. Climb the shared first pitch and the open-book corner of the Beckey ledge, then rejoin the Beckey Route for the final scramble and 5.6 friction slab to the summit.
wa_ridge_traverse_from_east_fury: From the Big Beaver landing, follow the nearly flat Big Beaver Trail about 9.4 miles up the valley to Luna Camp. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of the Access Creek confluence, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade.
Climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path up through the Access Creek basin to Access Col.
From Access Col, continue around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp.

From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier, over a possible bergschrund, to East Fury's summit. From there, descend loose talus west to the East Fury-West Fury saddle, where the towers begin.

Cross the towers. Bypass the first by about 100 ft of steep snow to a class 4 rock ramp, take scree ramps and a narrow ledge around the north side of the next, and make several low fifth-class moves through a notch. Downclimb or rappel off poor anchors around the remaining gendarmes, then traverse sloping slabs past more pinnacles to the true summit.
wa_rimrock_ridge_scramble: From State Route 20 at Marblemount, go straight onto the Cascade River Road where the highway turns, and drive it about 23 miles to its end at the large Cascade Pass parking lot at about 3,600 ft. The first third is paved, then gravel; the last few miles are narrow and steep. Camps on the traverse need an overnight backcountry permit.

Climb the Cascade Pass trail's switchbacks to Cascade Pass. From the pass, follow the traverse's climbers' path south on a rising traverse across the east slopes of Mixup Peak to the base of the Cache Glacier, climb its moderate snow to Cache Col, then make a descending traverse south-southeast to Kool-Aid Lake.

Head south from Kool-Aid Lake across the exposed Red Ledge below Arts Knoll, then rope up for the crevassed Middle Cascade Glacier and climb it to the Spider–Formidable col. Drop down the far side to Yang Yang Lakes.

Climb from the lakes back to the Le Conte ridge and up the Le Conte Glacier to the col between Le Conte and Sentinel at its head. Leave the traverse there, pass north of Sentinel Peak and follow the ridge east along its crest, the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek, to the summit. The ground is pathless cross-country alpine terrain.
wa_roan_wall_center_stage: Walk the old roadbed past a flagged landslide to the original road end, then 20-30 minutes on the old trail to a dry streambed about 50 ft wide full of white boulders, the last turnoff before the trail climbs south toward Squire Creek Pass. Drop about 200 ft down it, trend left into alders onto an informal path, follow it upvalley about 30 minutes to ford Squire Creek, then follow the fading track along the creek bed until the basin opens up.
wa_roan_wall_stage_right: Walk the old roadbed past a flagged landslide to the original road end, then 20-30 minutes on the old trail to a dry streambed about 50 ft wide full of white boulders, the last turnoff before the trail climbs south toward Squire Creek Pass. Drop about 200 ft down it, trend left into alders onto an informal path, follow it upvalley about 30 minutes to ford Squire Creek, then follow the fading track along the creek bed until the basin opens up.
wa_ruby_mountain_south_ridge: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east about 24 miles. Just past milepost 130, before the highway crosses the Thunder Arm of Diablo Lake, turn into Colonial Creek Campground and drive to the Thunder Creek Trailhead at the south end of the campground, at about 1,200 ft.

Hike the Thunder Creek Trail about 2 miles; a third of a mile past the bridge, turn left on the Fourth of July Pass Trail and climb steeply to the pass. Near a tall broken stump with old flagging, take the abandoned way trail off the north side northeast through forest, go straight up through blowdown and a rocky rib to a cairn near 4,950 ft, then follow the path up the south ridge and heather benches to open talus and the summit.
wa_ruth_icy_traverse: From Glacier, drive the Mount Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (Forest Road 32). Follow it 5.3 miles to the road end at Hannegan Campground and the trailhead at about 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
wa_sahale_mountain_r1: Walk the old mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile with almost no gain, past the derelict mine site, and watch for the cairned and flagged climbers' trail leaving the roadbed sharply to the right and going straight up; it is easy to walk past. The steep path switchbacks through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall to a series of small stream crossings in old-growth timber, the last reliable water before camp.
Keep climbing the steep, switchbacking climbers' path above the streams to treeline at about 5,300 ft, where the low camp sits on heather benches and moraine.
Continue up the path above the low camp toward Sharkfin Tower to the upper camps on the bench of slabs and grass at about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp, stay on climber's left and walk moraine and slabs toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower to the toe of the Quien Sabe Glacier. Rope up where the boot path meets continuous snow, around 6,700 ft.

Make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower onto the flatter part of the glacier, then pick a line up the steeper section between crevasses; the left-hand and more direct lines merge partway up. Cross near 7,600 ft on a snow bridge above and left of the bergschrund; the crossing point shifts from year to year.

Climb the upper glacier to a second crossing near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route late in the season. Later in summer the usual line goes right around the end of the bergschrund, then cuts back up and left to the Boston-Sahale col, the only low saddle at the top of the glacier.

From the col, traverse right (south) across a short but exposed snow slope with a rocky step, crampons and axe on and well back from any cornice, to the base of the summit block. Finish with about 60-70 ft of very exposed, loose Class 3 with 4th-class moves to the summit.
wa_sahale_mountain_sahale_glacier: Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the parking lot as it switchbacks steadily up through old-growth forest, roughly 1,800 ft in the first 2 miles, then eases across subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at about 3.7 miles.

At Cascade Pass take the left (north) fork signed for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, passing above Doubtful Lake. The final stretch above the Arm is loose scree and talus on cairns with real exposure, ending at the rock-walled tent pads of Sahale Glacier Camp.

From camp, rope up and climb the Sahale Glacier to the southwest base of the summit pyramid. A short, exposed stretch of steep snow and class 3-4 rock leads to a ledge just below the top, finished by an awkward chimney-like move onto the summit block.
wa_sews_sw_rib: From Winthrop drive west on Highway 20 about 31 miles and pass the Washington Pass Overlook; the Blue Lake Trailhead is on the left just under a mile beyond it. From Newhalem drive east about 42 miles; the trailhead is on the right before Washington Pass. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to a clearing. At a small, often cairned stream, leave the trail and follow climbers' tracks up the slabs beside the stream into the basin, then up talus to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the rib, just north of the Southwest Couloir. Climb the rib's seven pitches to the summit.
wa_sharkfin_tower_southeast_ridge: From the pullout, walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then turn sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. It climbs through old growth across four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the low camps, then continues up open heather and slabs to the higher camp on the meadow knoll.

From camp, skirt the climber's-left side of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it high, then rope up and traverse east along the top of the glacier until you are directly beneath the tower. Climb the single gully that breaks the rock band there (snow early season, loose scree later) to a terrace at the tower's base, then a short second gully to the notch. If your gully does not lead onto a terrace directly under the fin, you are in the wrong one.

From the notch, skirt the ridge on climber's right over large blocks and up a short dihedral to the crest, then follow the exposed crest and the upper blocks for about three pitches of low fifth class to the small summit.
wa_sheep_gap_mountain_scramble: From Granite Falls, follow the Mountain Loop Highway east about 11 miles to the Verlot Public Service Center, then about 19.3 miles more to Barlow Pass, where a parking lot with restrooms sits on the north side of the road. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Walk east along the highway about 200 ft to the gate and continue down the closed Monte Cristo Road, which parallels the Sauk River. After about three quarters of a mile, just before the road crosses the Sauk, take the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724 heading off to the right.
Follow Trail #724 on easy forest walking for about a mile to the Weden Creek ford, which can run high in snowmelt or after rain.
Beyond the ford the trail begins climbing steadily, switchbacking through forest; near mile 3.25 the tread turns noticeably rockier and steeper at the first of several creek gullies.
Keep climbing the rough, rocky trail across further gullies and talus slopes into Gothic Basin, where the small tarns below Foggy Lake mark the basin.

Leave the maintained tread and follow a flagged boot path west, re-crossing the Weden Creek outlet, then side-hill south across steep talus and heather benches for a bit over a mile to Weden Pass on the ridge crest.

From the pass, do not climb the first rock you see. Traverse southwest, dropping to about 4,900 ft on a brushy dirt ramp beneath the cliff bands, then regain height to the notch north of the main summit block. A saddle with two lower rock summits to its north is the wrong one.
From the notch, lead the short, steep class 4 step above it, protected with slings over horns and trees, then scramble the northeast ridge on loose class 3-4 rock and brush to the main summit.
wa_sherman_peak_baker_route: From the trailhead, follow Park Butte Trail #603 into Schriebers Meadow and across Sulphur Creek at the meadow's edge.

Stay on Park Butte Trail #603 past both Scott Paul Trail junctions, crossing the boulder fields of Rocky Creek and climbing through forest into Morovitz Meadow. About 2.4 miles from the trailhead, leave the Park Butte Trail and turn right onto Railroad Grade Trail #603.2; straight on leads to the Park Butte lookout instead.

Follow Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 onto the crest of the narrow lateral moraine and walk the spine past the designated camps and High Camp near 5,600 ft to Sandy Camp, where the maintained tread ends. The crest drops steeply on both sides in places.
From Sandy Camp, continue cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier and rope up.
Climb the Easton Glacier north, route-finding through the crevasse field and wanding the line for the descent, to the rim of Sherman Crater near 9,800 ft, where active fumaroles vent sulfurous steam.

Leave the main Easton line here and traverse the crater rim onto Sherman Peak's ridge, skirting a jagged high point, then climb the final steep snow (loose scree and rock when snow-free) to the small summit.
wa_sherman_peak_baker_squak_glacier: From SR-20 at milepost 82, about 16 miles east of Sedro-Woolley, turn north onto Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11). At about mile 12 turn left onto FS Road 12 and drive about 3.6 miles, then turn right onto FS Road 13 and follow it 5.3 miles to the Park Butte Trailhead at the road's end in Schriebers Meadow. A recreation pass is required to park.

Take the Scott Paul Trail #603.1, which branches off the Park Butte Trail about 100 ft from the trailhead, and follow it through forest and meadows. Leave it north at an unmarked junction on a steep climbers' path to the toe of the Squak Glacier, where high camp is usually set near 6,500 ft. Rope up and climb the crevassed Squak Glacier north toward Sherman Peak, then steep, often icy slopes to its summit ridge and the top.
wa_silver_star_northwest_face: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) over Washington Pass and continue east about 4 miles, down past the hairpin, to a broad shoulder and pullout near milepost 165-166 that looks straight across the Early Winters Creek valley at Silver Star. No parking pass or permit is needed. The highway over Washington Pass closes for winter, so early- and late-season access depends on the road being open.
wa_silver_star_west_face_couloir: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) over Washington Pass and continue east about 4 miles, down past the hairpin, to a broad shoulder and pullout near milepost 165-166 that looks straight across the Early Winters Creek valley at Silver Star. No parking pass or permit is needed. The highway over Washington Pass closes for winter, so early- and late-season access depends on the road being open.
wa_sinister_peak_north_face: From the Darrington Ranger Station, drive SR 530 north about 8 miles and turn right (east) onto Suiattle River Road (FR 26). Follow it about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead at about 1,440 ft, just past the Downey Creek bridge; park on the right (south) side, and the trail starts on the left. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is required, and a free Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead.

Hike Downey Creek Trail #768 about 6.5 miles to the camp near 2,440 ft, then take the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, fording to the south side near 3,700 ft, over a pass near 5,900 ft to high camp on the ridge above the lake. Cross the col between the two glaciers near 8,500 ft, descend onto the Chickamin Glacier and traverse east beneath the peak to the bergschrund, then climb the 45-50 degree face and a short rock scramble to the summit.
wa_skeena26: Follow the old roadbed beyond the gate past the landslide crossing to two cut logs on either side of the road with old logging cable showing, where a boot track drops right toward the creek. Ford Squire Creek at its shallowest point, follow the climbers' track upstream across a tributary, then climb two steep, muddy gullies to the open grassy saddle below the wall.
wa_skookum_peak_twinsisters_scramble: Follow Elbow Lake Trail #697 about 0.2 mile from the trailhead to the Middle Fork Nooksack River. There is no bridge here, so it is a ford that can be impassable at high water.

Beyond the river, continue on the Elbow Lake Trail as it climbs to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaves the trail. It is easy to walk past, so watch for paint blazes and flagging.
Follow the climbers' path west up the Green Creek drainage to the mouth of the Green Creek Cirque, where the creek is the last reliable water before the upper slabs and ridge.
Scramble loose third- and fourth-class ground out of the cirque to gain the ridge crest just south of South Twin, where the rock turns to grippy olivine.
wa_sloan_peak_corkscrew: Walk the old Bedal Creek Trail about 1.5 miles and 700 ft to around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path, often marked with pink flagging, turns off to the left. Watch for it: the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

Climb the path steeply through forest to talus near 4,900 ft, then bend southeast to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Continue southeast over a rock ridge near 5,800 ft, rope up and cross the Sloan Glacier southwest to the rock near 7,100 ft. Follow the exposed heather shelf of the Corkscrew across the south face onto the west face, climb the gully to the crest, then a short class 4 step and third class to the summit.
wa_south_arete: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway (closed over Washington Pass in winter), to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead near milepost 161, just west of Washington Pass: about 42 miles east of Newhalem, or about 30 miles west of Winthrop. Park in the lot at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day pass is required.

Follow Blue Lake Trail #314 about 1.3 to 1.5 miles to a minor stream draining the basin below the Early Winters Spires, well short of Blue Lake, and leave the trail on the cairned climbers' path. Follow it up slabs, heather and talus beside the stream to the southwest toe of South Early Winters Spire, then climb the South Arete, a short slab crux, a chimney and the broken crest, to the summit.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_direct_east_: Drive SR-20 to Washington Pass (the highway is closed over the pass in winter), then continue east, downhill, to the big hairpin switchback just below the pass; from the Mazama side it is the hairpin you reach as the road climbs to the pass. Park in the dirt pullout at the hairpin, about 5,100 ft, directly below the east faces of the Early Winters Spires. This is not the Blue Lake Trailhead.

Hike up Spire Gully, following occasional cairns, to the last large tree in the middle of the gully, then traverse right across talus (snow early in the season) to below the gully that leads to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires. Traverse left to the foot of the east buttress and climb its nine pitches to the summit.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_passenger: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway (closed over Washington Pass in winter), to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead near milepost 161, just west of Washington Pass: about 42 miles east of Newhalem, or about 30 miles west of Winthrop. Park in the lot at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day pass is required.

Follow Blue Lake Trail #314 to the climbers' path and take it up to the base of the South Arete. From there head down and right along the base of the wall for about 10 minutes, losing some height to skirt steeper ground, to double cracks beside a fir tree; the four-bolt dihedral 100 ft farther on is the neighboring route. Climb the seven pitches to the South Arete and follow it to the summit.
wa_south_early_winter_spire_southwest_co: Drive SR-20, the North Cascades Highway (closed over Washington Pass in winter), to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead near milepost 161, just west of Washington Pass: about 42 miles east of Newhalem, or about 30 miles west of Winthrop. Early in the season the lot may still hold snow. A Northwest Forest Pass or day pass is required.

Follow Blue Lake Trail #314 about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path and take it up into the basin west of the Liberty Bell group. Enter the couloir about 100 ft below the start of the South Arete, on its left, climb the wide lower gully, take the right branch at the fork through the narrowing, and from the small saddle at its top make one low fifth-class move and scramble to the summit.
wa_south_face: Vasiliki Tower stands on the left (north) side as you enter the col. From the col, scramble up broken ground to the system of right-trending dihedrals on the tower's sunny south face and follow them for two pitches to the summit.
wa_south_face_2: Park at the unsigned roadside pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about 4 miles east of Washington Pass. Follow the climbers' path down through boulders and talus, losing about 200 ft, to Early Winters Creek, and cross it on logs.

Past the creek, follow the climbers' path up the timbered rib on the north side of Burgundy Creek, climbing steeply about 2,300 ft to the broad bench camp at about 6,500 ft, the staging area for the Wine Spires.
From the bench, continue up the climbers' path through scree gullies, snow early in the season, to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft.
wa_south_face_3: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is required, and the small lot fills early. SR-20 over the pass is closed in winter.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the climbers' path on the left at a large cairn. Work up and left into the Concord-Lexington gully, not the Liberty Bell-Concord one, using the path along its left side to the Concord-Lexington notch. From the notch, traverse the gravelly ledges on Concord's side and climb the three pitches of the South Face, over the Shark Fin, to the summit.
wa_south_face_4: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the large turnout on the hairpin switchback just east of Washington Pass, at about 5,100 ft, the same pullout used for the Hairpin Crags and the other Kangaroo Ridge climbs. SR-20 over the pass is closed in winter.

Follow the faint, cairned climbers' trail south across the boulder field, through forest and more talus to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour. Do not head up the gully toward the notch between the Temple and Little Finger; instead drop some height below the pass and traverse across to the base of the South Face, then climb its seven pitches, finishing up a V-slot to the summit.
wa_south_face_5: Drive SR-20 east from I-5 about 60 miles to Newhalem. Just after crossing Goodell Creek, turn left onto the small road to the Goodell Creek campgrounds and follow it uphill to the Upper Goodell Creek Group Camp at about 600 ft; the trail starts just back down the road from the camp. Camping in Terror Basin needs a national park backcountry permit, picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.

Follow the trail's old roadbed about 4 miles, across two boulder washouts, to a fire-ring campsite 200 yards past the second; take the unsigned boot path right, steeply through forest to treeline near 5,000 ft, traverse to the 6,200 ft saddle near Glee Peak and drop to camp near 5,800 ft. Rope up, cross the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the face's lower-left corner, and climb four pitches via the Great Gash to the summit.
wa_south_face_center: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of the highway, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass and roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is required, and the small lot fills early. SR-20 over the pass is closed in winter.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the climbers' path on the left at a large cairn. Work up and left into the Concord-Lexington gully, not the Liberty Bell-Concord one, using the path along its left side to the Concord-Lexington notch. From the notch, climb the obvious crack up the middle of Concord's south face through a bulge, then trend left through two right-facing corners to the summit block.
wa_south_ridge: From Darrington, drive SR-530 north about 8 miles to the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26) and follow it east about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead, at about 1,450 ft. The trail starts just past the Downey Creek bridge on the north side of the road; parking is on the south side. The Suiattle River Road is prone to washout closures, so check its status before going.
wa_south_ridge_3: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR 20) to Rainy Pass near milepost 157.5, about 50 miles east of Marblemount or 35 miles west of Winthrop, and turn into the Rainy Pass Picnic Area on the south side of the highway; the Lake Ann/Maple Pass trailhead sign is at the north end of the lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required. The highway closes for the winter over the pass.

Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1.3 miles through forest to the signed fork, stay right toward Heather Pass (the left fork goes to Lake Ann), and climb through meadows to Heather Pass, where you leave the maintained trail for the unmarked climbers' path toward Lewis and Wing Lakes.

Follow the unmarked, cairned climbers' path west from Heather Pass across two loose talus and boulder fields. The cairns are easy to lose in fog or under early-season snow, and this is the main route-finding problem of the approach.
Beyond the second talus field, drop down to Lewis Lake. The few tent sites are in the timber on the north shore.
From Lewis Lake, climb about 1,200 ft of meadow and talus west to Wing Lake.
The established tent sites are in the trees on the right as you reach the lake, beside the outlet.

Go around the right (north) side of Wing Lake, climb the moraine and permanent snowfield into the obvious talus and snow gully below the col, and angle climber's right out of it near the top to avoid the cliff bands directly below the col.
From the col, scramble north along the cairned south ridge toward the summit pyramid; a short class 4 step of about 15 ft guards the top.
wa_south_ridge_4: From camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the glacier's flank (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline from camp, below an obvious crack leading to a U-shaped notch. Climb the crack to the notch, cross to the far side and climb cracks back to the knife-edge crest, follow the crest two pitches to a short downclimb, then scramble the broad upper ridge to the summit.
wa_south_ridge_6: From WA-20 in Marblemount, turn onto Cascade River Road and drive about 22 miles, paved at first and then gravel, to a small pullout on the left opposite Johannesburg Mountain at about 3,200 ft, shortly after milepost 22. If you reach the Cascade Pass road end you have gone too far. Overnight stays in Boston Basin need a North Cascades National Park wilderness permit.

Climb the steep, unmaintained climbers' path from the pullout along the old mine roadbed, across several streams and out above treeline to the Boston Basin camps near 6,400 ft. From camp, go up the snowfields to the foot of the formation's left-hand (south) skyline, leave the snow and climb about five pitches along the crest, passing a gendarme on its right side, to the summit.
wa_south_spur: From Glacier, drive SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) about 13 miles east and, just before the bridge over the Nooksack River, turn left onto FS Road 32. At 1.3 miles keep left on Ruth Creek Road and drive 5.4 miles to the road end at Hannegan Campground and the trailhead, about 3,100 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Hike Trail #674 about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, descend past Boundary Camp, ford the Chilliwack River and climb the old Easy Ridge path to Easy Saddle. Follow the ridge over Easy Peak, past the Imperfect Impasse (often bypassed by dropping to about 4,400 ft and climbing an exposed class 4 step), to Perfect Pass, then climb north up the south snowfield to the col and the short, exposed crest to the summit.
wa_south_twin_sister_north_ridge: From I-5 Exit 255, drive SR 542 east about 16.7 miles and turn right on Mosquito Lake Road. After 4.8 miles, just past Porter Creek, turn left on Middle Fork Road (FS Road 38), follow it 4.8 miles, and turn right at the junction that drops to the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at about 1,200 ft. Most parties bike the logging roads beyond the gate.

Bike the logging roads around Dailey Prairie to the road end below the cirque between the Twins, then follow the brushy climbers' path southeast through timber and talus, past old cabin ruins, to Orsino Creek (last water). Grind up scree into the basin and keep higher and left to the 5,800-ft saddle between North and South Twin, cross the Sisters Glacier onto the north ridge, and follow the crest to the summit.
wa_south_twin_sister_scramble: From I-5 Exit 255, drive SR 542 east about 16.7 miles and turn right on Mosquito Lake Road. After 4.8 miles, just past Porter Creek, turn left on Middle Fork Road (FS Road 38), follow it 4.8 miles, and turn right at the junction that drops to the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at about 1,200 ft. Most parties bike the logging roads beyond the gate.

Bike the logging roads around Dailey Prairie into the basin between the Twins and follow the climbers' path through forest and talus, past old cabin ruins, to Orsino Creek Basin (last water). Climb the loose gully and talus to the 5,200-ft notch in the West Ridge, scramble the ridge east to the high notch near 6,600 ft, then traverse right across the snowfield or scree to the southern gullies and climb them to the summit.
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner: From SR 20 at milepost 82 near Concrete, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive about 24 miles to FS Road 1152, directly across from Shannon Creek Campground. Turn left on 1152, then take a sharp right onto spur 1152-014 and follow it to the road end at about 2,500 ft. The gravel can be potholed but is passable to most cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass is required to park.

Climb the Shannon Ridge trail east-northeast up the ridge to the 5,400 ft pass where the Sulphide Glacier first comes into view, then continue up the open snow to the large flat plateau at about 6,400 ft at the edge of the glacier. The featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft is hard to navigate in poor visibility.
wa_southern_man: Drive SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) to about half a mile east of Washington Pass and park in the dirt pullout at the obvious hairpin turn, at about 5,100 ft, directly below the east faces of the Early Winters Spires. This is the east-side start, not the Blue Lake trailhead west of the pass.

Hike up the cairned Spire Gully to the last large tree, traverse right across talus (snow early season) to the gully that leads to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress before reaching the notch. Climb the shared Direct East Buttress pitches, break out left about halfway up onto the south-facing headwall, and follow its crack pitches to the summit.
wa_sperry_peak_standard: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 28 miles (about 17 miles past the Verlot Public Service Center) and turn right onto Sunrise Mine Road, FS Road 4065. Follow it about 2.2 miles to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, about 2,350 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass is required to park.
wa_spider_mountain_north_face: From SR 20 at Marblemount, cross the Skagit River bridge onto Cascade River Road and follow it about 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead lot, about 3,660 ft. The upper miles are gravel.
wa_southwest_buttress: From high camp, rope up and cross north over the Inspiration Glacier to the col at about 8,000 ft where it meets the McAllister Glacier.
From the col, drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier and descend toward its southwest gap, threading the visible crevasses, which open up late in the season.

Continue across the McAllister to the Marble Creek-McAllister pass, the lowest gap on the southwest side of the glacier, and cross onto the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.
wa_spontaneity_arete: From the west end of the turnout, follow the cairned climbers' trail steeply down into the trees, cross Early Winters Creek on logs, and climb the rocky drainage and talus toward the formation; most parties take the newer variation that bears right just before the old fixed lines. Start at the dead snags on the left before the gully and climb the arete's seven pitches, with long class 3 scrambles between them, to the top of the technical climbing.
Scramble about 200 to 300 ft of class 3 along the crest, with one exposed 4th-class move near the top, to the summit.
wa_superalpine: From Darrington, drive the Mountain Loop Highway south about 17 miles and turn left onto FR 4096, about a mile past Bedal Campground. Climb the steep, narrow road about 2 miles to its end at roughly 2,800 ft; high clearance is recommended. The road is not plowed, so in a normal winter skinning starts well below the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 up the Bedal Creek valley to the meadow at about 5,000 ft beneath the west face, normally a 4 to 5 hour skin in winter. Climb the spur ridge west of the peak to about 5,700 ft, leave skis, and take the obvious ice line on the right side of the face, a WI4 curtain then fat WI3 in the main gully, to the upper snowfields and up them to the summit.
wa_sw_couloir_and_face: From Bellingham, drive SR-542 (Mount Baker Highway) east past Glacier and up past Heather Meadows to the Lake Ann Trailhead lot, about 1 mile below Artist Point at roughly 4,700 ft. The upper highway is usually snowbound until early summer. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.
Take Lake Ann Trail #600 as it descends into the upper Swift Creek basin, then climb out of the basin to the saddle above Lake Ann and drop to the lake, about 4 miles.

From the lake, follow the climbers' path toward the Fisher Chimneys. Before reaching the Chimneys, traverse right (east) onto the crevassed Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it up to the upper southeast corner of the basin, where the glacier runs out against the mountain at the foot of the icefall.
wa_sw_ridge: There is no road to Stehekin. Take the Lady of the Lake ferry up Lake Chelan from Chelan to Stehekin, then ride the park shuttle about 11 miles up the Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge, where the Pacific Crest Trail heads up Agnes Creek.

Follow the Pacific Crest Trail and Agnes Creek trail about 9 to 10 miles, cross Agnes Creek on a log, and bushwhack steeply about 5,000 ft into the upper Blue Glacier basin to a high camp on the rock ridge above the glacier, below the east side of the Gunsight peaks. From camp, work around to the west side of the towers and climb the Southwest Ridge to the summit.
wa_swiss_peak_standard_route: From I-5 Exit 230 at Burlington, follow SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, east through Marblemount and past Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking area near milepost 134, about 28 miles beyond Marblemount. Any overnight stay requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, reserved in advance or picked up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
wa_table_mountain_standard_scramble: From I-5 Exit 255 in Bellingham, follow SR 542, the Mount Baker Highway, east through Glacier and past the Mt. Baker Ski Area and Heather Meadows to the road's end at the Artist Point parking lot, about 5,100 ft. The last stretch opens only once the snow is cleared, usually in summer. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required to park.

From the northwest corner of the lot, opposite the vault toilets, take Table Mountain Trail #681 up the tight switchbacks cut into the southeast-face cliff band, about 400 ft of exposed tread, onto the flat plateau. Follow the main path west-northwest along the south rim, ignoring the braided use-trails, about 1.4 miles in all to the high point.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast: Hike White River Trail #1507 up the valley about 4 miles to the Boulder Creek crossing and the junction with the Boulder Creek Trail to Boulder Pass. Stay on the White River Trail.
Continue up the White River Trail about 2 more miles to the Thunder Creek crossing, where there is an established camp.

Find the old, unmaintained sheep path that leaves the White River Trail near the Thunder Creek crossing and climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. It is hard to find, and the tread is choked with avalanche debris, blowdown and dense slide alder up to about 5,000 ft.
From the col, climb the loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Test every hold and keep the party out of each other's fall line.
From the ledge, climb the face to the broken chimney and follow its jam crack, Class 4 to easy Class 5, about 50 to 100 ft to the summit.
wa_tepeh_towers: Walk back a short way along the road to the current crossing of the Cascade River, a log or a braided ford that shifts year to year, then climb the steep unmaintained climbers' path through old growth to a boulder field, cross Eldorado Creek and continue into the Eldorado Creek basin meadows. Rope up and climb the Eldorado Glacier to the camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet.
Rope up and walk the glacier north-northwest for about 45 minutes to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arete that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.
wa_the_cave_route: From Winthrop, drive SR 20 west about 30 miles, over Washington Pass, to the signed Blue Lake Trailhead about a mile west of the pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required to park.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, take the climbers' path just past a small stream, and climb slabs, talus and meadow up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, often snowy and icy into late June. From the notch drop about 50 ft down the gully on Concord's north side to two diagonal cracks, and climb the three pitches through the cave to the summit.
wa_the_chalice: From Winthrop, drive SR 20 west about 18 miles to Forest Road 5310-200 on the left, between mileposts 176 and 175 and about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. Follow it to the road end by a gravel pit, at about 3,000 ft; the trail starts near the pit entrance. A Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required.

Hike Cedar Creek Trail #476 about 5 miles; below the old burn turn right onto a rough path up the right side of the creek draining the Silver Horn's south side, to meadows near 6,200 ft and the pale granite face. The Chalice takes the right side of the face to a broad mid-height ledge, walks left along it, climbs left of the central arete and finishes on blocky ground right of the summit chimney.
wa_the_chopping_block_south_route: Hike the old Goodell Creek Trail, a former logging-road bed that is overgrown in places with downed trees and small creek crossings, up-valley about 4 miles to a flat spot marked by cairns, where the unmaintained Terror Basin climbers' path leaves the roadbed and climbs steeply up the slope to the right.
wa_the_devils_club: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead near milepost 134, about 14 miles past Newhalem, and park in the small lot. From here a trail drops about 1 mile through forest toward Ross Dam; at the bottom, turn right on the gravel road to the lakeshore, where a phone on the last power pole calls Ross Lake Resort for the water taxi, which must be reserved in advance.
wa_the_hitchhiker: Drive SR-20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at milepost 161, on the south side of the highway about 1 mile west of Washington Pass. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and the highway over the pass is closed in winter, usually from about November to April.

Take the Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path to the base of the South Arete, about 1 hour, then traverse down and right along the base of the wall past the Passenger's fir-tree and double-crack start and roughly 100 ft farther to a small left-facing dihedral with four bolts. Climb nine pitches of sustained face and crack up the southeast face to the summit.
wa_the_needle_neve_glacier: Follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail about 2.1 miles and 1,500 ft up through forest to the lake, where the maintained trail ends.

Pick up the unmaintained climbers' path around the east (right) side of the lake. It climbs steep, root-laced forest for about 2,000 ft before opening into heather and boulders, then gains the narrowing ridge crest above the lake.

Follow the narrowing ridge, then traverse scree and boulders, snow-covered into midsummer, below Pyramid Peak's steep east-face cliffs to the flat bench beside the moraine lake at the toe of the Colonial Glacier, about 6,100 ft.
Rope up and climb south up the Colonial Glacier on snow of about 30 degrees, skirting the moraine lake, to the col at about 6,900 ft.
Descend about 200 to 250 ft down the far side of the col onto the Neve Glacier and head across it, roped, on a middle line toward Snowfield Peak; open crevasses are scattered across its east side.
Continue up the Neve toward Snowfield Peak to about 7,700 ft, where the route leaves the Snowfield line and turns west along the glacier's rim below Horseman's Pack.

Work west along the ice edge past Horseman's Pack and The Horseman, then turn north along the rim to the snow arete that runs up to the southeast ridge. Turn or bridge the bergschrund at its foot, follow the ridge north and then west around a corner on exposed class 3, and cross the knife-edge below the top with a few low class-5 moves to the summit.
wa_the_pleiades_scramble: The isthmus camp sits on the strip of ground between the two Twin Lakes, a few minutes' walk from the road end.
Start up the Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from between the lakes and, a short way up, bear right at the signed junction onto High Pass Trail #676; the left fork climbs to the Winchester lookout.
Follow High Pass Trail #676 as it traverses below Winchester Mountain, dropping about 300 ft to cross a steep avalanche chute that can hold snow into August.
Continue on the trail past the chute, climbing over Low Pass and on to High Pass, the broad saddle on the ridge crest.

Leave the trail and climb the scree or snow slope NNE about 400-500 ft to the col in Larrabee's south arm. Descend slightly from the col, traverse the basin about half a mile, then climb the loose, narrow gully to the notch between the first and second Pleiades.

From the notch, scramble up to the goat ledge and traverse it east; a little over halfway along, leave the ledge and scramble loose 3rd/4th-class rock to the third Pleiad, the high point of the group.
wa_the_pyramid_picket_south_route: Hike the Goodell Creek climbers' trail, an old logging-road grade that parallels the creek, a little over 4 miles to where the road tread ends at a rock arrow, post and large cairn marking the Terror Creek climbers' trail.

Turn east onto the unmaintained climbers' trail and climb steeply through timber; higher up the faint, brushy path works through a cliff band with Class 3 root-pull sections where the tread is easy to lose.
Above the cliff band, break out onto open heather and talus and work up and west to the flat, gravelly basin at treeline with running water.

From camp, cross heather benches, loose rock and moats west to the upper Barrier notch at about 6,200 ft. Use this upper crossing, not the lower Stump Hollow one, which sets you up under a different peak.
